records.title: IGA "AIDE GOURMET"
records.description: Jean-Sebastien Guillemette, 3D artist at Shed in Montreal: "We had to create the concepts, storyboard, animatic and final rendered animation from a scenario the agency Sid Lee wrote. The story followed a client asking an IGA employee what he could do with an eggplant. "The character designs were of great concern to the clients because even though the goal was to deliver a cartoonish animation, the character couldn't look too funny. The whole project had to be balanced between cartoon and realism. "The quantity of detail in the environment and the quantity of characters to create from scratch were definitely a challenge in the time we had. "We used Softimage as our primary 3D software. Everything was rendered in Arnold and composited in Nuke. We have our own in-house renderfarm to process the whole thing." Schedule: "We had a little bit more than two months from the time we received the brief and delivered the project."

records.title: PETA "98% HUMAN"
records.description: The Mill+ animation director Angus Kneale: "'98% Human' is part of PETA's commitment to stop primates being used within the entertainment industries as actors. We embarked on an incredibly ambitious journey to create a truly photo-real 100 percent CGI chimpanzee. "This was one of the most exciting and challenging projects I've ever worked on. Crafting PETA '98% Human' was more than about creating a totally believable, CG chimp. It was about establishing an emotional connection and empathy with the audience. "In the past we would have used motion capture and mapped a human actor's performance directly onto the CG character. But we wanted to approach this project in a different way, so we decided to rely on the skill of our animators for the final chimp performances, only using an actor for pre-vis. "We pushed computer graphics imagery to a new level creating bespoke technology in muscle and skin simulation, higher than any other project or film to date. "We achieved this by developing new techniques from simulated bloodstreams, skin tension and even individual pores at the base of every hair on the chimpanzee, all with the aim to create a creature that is practically indistinguishable from his flesh and blood counterpart. The spot demonstrates the partnership between creativity and technology by delivering on PETA's powerful message that you do not need to use live primates as actors, now that we can create fully life-like, photo-real primates."

records.title: WORKSAFE "NICK"
records.description: Lara Allen, producer at Resolution in Sydney: "Young workers - apprentices, part timers, casual workers, etc. - simply don't believe the workplace can be dangerous, but they are at extremely high risk of accidents. "Most of these accidents are due to being inexperienced, unsure, over-confident and embarrassed about speaking up. "Our goal was to give director Josh Frizzell total freedom to get the performance and camera action he wanted, while we solved the problems and complexities of each VFX shot in post." "To keep the performances natural, the director had to move fairly quickly, and at times this meant we didn't get all of the special effects plates we would have liked for compositing. Having said that, we were totally supportive of this approach to the shoot. "Luckily we had the schedule to finesse the most difficult shots until everyone was happy. We largely used Nuke and 2D solutions to get the effects plates to blend into the live action. "The other big challenge was to grade the footage so that a sense of time could be conveyed without the usual problems that flashback sequences often have in film. We wanted a very naturalistic style, and, with a lot of fine tuning, we got there."

records.title: HARRODS "FINE WATCH ROOM"
records.description: Creative team at Mainframe in London: "The client came to us with a fairly open concept: a nest of ants work together to create the Harrods logo using parts from watch movements. "Mainframe was responsible for creating the flow and narrative of the spot, concentrating on camera moves and set-ups, trying to create shots that would draw the viewer into the story and emphasize the macro scale of the scenes. "We were lucky to find some amazing ant reference footage from a BBC documentary. This proved vital for the last two shots where they interact in the piles or 'death spiral', as it is known in ant circles. "We predominantly use Maya but the ant pile shot required more complicated dynamic simulations, which was taken care of with PFlow in 3ds Max. The rest of the ant flocking animation was made using nParticles, curve flow and instanced geometry with walk cycles in Maya. "We rendered using V-Ray in Maya and used Nuke to composite, then added Video Copilot optical flares for some finishing touches. "The most demanding technical aspect of this project surrounded the scale of the piece. Starting in macro before pulling out and revealing the enormity of the swarm, thousands of ants, all working together. This was achieved using a V-Ray proxy/Maya particle combo. "The proxies in V-Ray allow a huge number of objects to be in a scene, whilst only displaying a fraction of the faces actually present. This makes moving around the viewport and generally working with the scene bearable, without which it would be chug central. "Our workflow involved a generic walk-cycle instanced as a V-Ray proxy in the particle system with tweaks to the movement so the pace of the ants matched the cycle. " We used the same technique for the cogs in the logo, which was modeled then converted after animation and reimported into the scene as a proxy."

records.title: ZERO HUNGER CHALLENGE "HUNGER IS A TYRANT"
records.campaign_title: ZERO HUNGER CHALLENGE "HUNGER IS A TYRANT"
records.description: Helmed by Platige director Damian Nenow and narrated by Dakota Fanning, this powerful spot leads off the UN-sponsored Hunger Personified campaign designed "to highlight the dangers of being apathetic to hunger and accepting it as a necessary evil." Damian Nenow: "When I was approached with the challenge of depicting hunger as a ruthless tyrant, I was intrigued. I think the heightened level of emotion in the clip is justified, given the number of lives wasted needlessly by hunger when it's clearly a problem that can be eradicated. "The Zero Hunger Challenge was launched at the Rio+20 summit in June 2012 by Secretary General of the United Nations, Ban Ki-moon calling on leaders, business and civil society to step up efforts to end hunger – emphasizing that almost one billion people still go to bed hungry each day, saying food security was a top priority."

records.title: JOSE CUERVO CINGE "STING"
records.description: Andy Hall, director at Elastic in Santa Monica: "The agency asked us to conceive of an animation style or identity that could be owned by the brand while conveying a clear and concise fable-genre based story. "Finding a unique look for anything these days is a challenge. Most of what we see being done is referential to a degree. So we spent some time developing that look so that it could be our own. "As a studio, we're not necessarily known for doing traditional 2D animation but we pride ourselves on pushing our limits and always reinventing our style. So we worked from within, using our talents and applying what we know about animation to the 2D execution. "Also, we had to find a way to retain the very graphic look of the concept art within the animation while taking it to another level. There were a lot of mediums that we worked across and they all had to live within the same graphic language. "In developing the look we had to keep in mind it needed to translate into print, point of sale, posters, and a graphic novel that was printed for use by their sales force. The graphic novel is designed and the story told in the true style of the genre. All of the artwork and storytelling was designed by our team at Elastic." Schedule: six weeks.

records.title: JARRITOS "GLASSBLOWERS"
records.description: Director Ryan Dunn at CHRLX in NY: "It's always been a goal of mine to effectively emulate the analog world in a digital space. Many have tried it, myself included, but I think we've gotten really close here. "Suspending viewer disbelief was the key to the campaign, so we put a lot of effort into creating a seamless experience without the distraction of the technique itself. "Whether or not it could be done the way I pictured it in my head was another story. I had a full stop-motion team on standby up until our CG crew showed me a proof of concept that blew us all away. "The Jarritos scripts were inspired by the miniatures and dioramas created by artist Tamra Kohl, and the agency wanted to match the original look. They also wanted the flexibility of revisions, something for which full stop-motion was not very amenable. "After I saw what our CG team could do, I knew that our process needed to combine digital characters with analog sets, and it turned out to be the perfect choice for our client's needs and the end product. "Our characters had to look, feel, and act the part so we focused heavily on the performance of our digital actors and made sure that the spaces they occupied held up to the curiosity of the campaign's overall concept."

records.title: KRAKEN BLACK SPICED RUM "BLACK INK"
records.description: In a departure from the 2D woodblock print style of previous Kraken Rum spots created by Brooklyn's Transistor, this entirely CG commercial for 'The Kraken Rum' directed by Tim Miller of Blur Studio ("Deadpool") provides a visceral portrayal of the legendary sea creature for which the Caribbean spiced rum is named. The agency Dead As We Know It, approached the Blur to create the visuals for this spot after seeing the Studio's work on "The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo" opening titles. Schedule: 10 weeks.

records.title: BRITISH GAS "ACTIVE HEATING", "LLAMAS"
records.description: Buck creative director Ryan Honey in LA: "Nothing sells next generation thermostat control like a conglomerate of cockamamie critters cavorting around the United Kingdom. In this campaign for British Gas, we teamed up with the kooky folks at CHI & Partners to bring a little happy to heating your home. "Each character has been depicted in a simple, hand-drawn style with splashes of color consistent with the Hive brand. The animation – a combination of cel and 3D – is designed to appear seamless, with the line art flowing from one element to another in a smooth continuous motion."

records.title: TINE MILK "WINTER OLYMPICS"
records.description: Mill+ art director Antar Walker in London: "This was a unique project combining traditional hand animation, 3D, camera projection and compositing to tell a Norwegian folklore tale with a modern twist. "Taking influence from famous Norwegian illustrator Theodor Kittelsen, we see the icy world brought to life by our team of Flash, Cinema 4D and After Effects artists. "The project was a technical challenge and offered a chance to experiment with different animation techniques, as well as develop the visual style along the way."

records.title: DORSET CEREALS "LIFE BEGINS AT BREAKFAST"
records.description: Nexus director Conor Finnegan leverages the charm and subtle humor of his multi-award-winning short film "Fear of Flying" for this gentle peek at a wooly, puppet-populated woodland thru London Agency Sunshine for Dorset Cereal. Conor Finnegan: "The brief was to create a world where Mike, a bird DJ who works at Dorset AM, wakes the nation with his early morning radio show, Dawn Chorus. "It was a tight enough schedule from initial go-ahead, with just two weeks for model/character-maker Jessica Dance to create all 18 characters (each one lovingly crafted in 100% organic British lambswool). "Meanwhile, Andy Gent and his team were creating the miniature sets and props that make up the film. We had a two-day shoot at Clapham Road studios where we shot all the puppets live-action on set, puppeteering them on sticks and creating walk-cycles with lumpy wheels. After the shoot it was back to Nexus HQ where we began adding all the 2D animated arms, legs, wings, eyes and 3D beaks, etc."

records.title: OHSU "ONE DOWN: MAKE CANCER THE VICTIM"
records.campaign_title: OHSU "ONE DOWN: MAKE CANCER THE VICTIM"
records.description: Robert Sethi, director and creative director at the The Mill+: "We had the honour of collaborating with Wieden+Kennedy on Oregon Health & Science University's (OHSU) new campaign outlining how OHSU revolutionised the treatment of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia, making a once lethal disease non-lethal for hundreds of thousands of people. "And having taken one cancer down, they're going after the rest. "This piece is inspired by reality without trying to replicate it. Whilst we did a lot of research to understand cells and cancer, we used it more for inspiration. "Instead of individually sculpting each cell we used a set of noise and rules to randomly generate them, giving us a lot more freedom. And the comp team, led by Martin Karlsson, did a really excellent job. They took our renders and really pushed the electro-microscope effect to the maximum." "Initially it's a darker world which progressively lightens as the cancer explodes and disappears. The colors shift and the camera goes from static to loose movements, all conveying this sense of hopefulness and victory. "It was an incredibly gratifying piece to work on not just from an artistic point of view; everyone has a loved one that's been affected by cancer, so working on a project that might help people in the future was a very rewarding thing."

records.title: ECHO "TROLLS"
records.description: Pablo Tufaro, director at Laposta in Buenos Aires, Argentina: "The fact this client was very open minded was the most attractive part of this project. And they wanted to do some nasty humor with disgusting and disturbing trolls disturbing the owner of the garden because he has abandoned it." "The script was awesome, very good jokes all the time but the best part was when the actors that made the voices started to improvise. That was hilarious. "That's when we decided to do an extended version of the commercial with a couple more jokes than the original script. "There were many technical challenges: muscle systems, facial expression tracking, long hair with dynamics, three characters at the same time on a two-month deadline. "For sure, the creative challenge was finding the best people around the world to help us make this commercial outstanding. "The rig was made in Canada, the retopology and UV was made in Spain, one animator from Colombia, another from Mexico and the live action was shot in the US. "We are a Softimage studio, even if it's dead software, it's so fast and versatile that it will be difficult to stop using it. We render with Arnold. Those are our most powerful tools."

records.title: MONEY SUPERMARKET "ELEPHUNK"
records.description: MPC say they channeled Samuel L Jackson, John Travolta, Michael Jackson and Beyonce to choreograph the moves of this funky 15-foot African bull elephant strutting the streets of Vancouver. MPC 3D supervisor Fabian Frank: "The biggest challenge was creating an elephant that could pull out the moves with the best of them, yet was also believable and true to life. We solved this by ensuring his dance moves stayed within the realms of what a real elephant could do. "The second challenge came with integrating the elephant into the shot footage. Matching the interaction between the talent and the elephant were key, so the talent was tracked and rotoscoped back into the shots – using select takes to perfectly match the elephant's walk cycle." "MPC's 3D team began to concept their elephant two weeks prior to the shoot. A pre-vis laying out his size and basic flow of movement was then used as a guide for the rig on set. "Following the shoot, the team decided upon the look of the elephant and his subsequent texture. They settled on the male African elephant, embarking on the creation of an exact replica with added personality. "As part of this creative process, the intricacies of elephant mobility and human dance moves were studied. A number of dance variations and moves were tested in order to create his final choreographed routine. "A range of detailed matte paintings were also developed, adding skyscrapers and lights to emphasis the 'epic' feel of the backdrop for our VIP's."

records.title: VOLVIC "GIANT"
records.description: David Danesi, VFX producer at Digital District in Paris: "Volvic wanted to give its brand a new image, more modern, more edgy. They wanted so see water and also the color green in the commercial. "The main creative challenge was to create a very graphic universe. There was a lot of tests and artistic direction research in order to find a real and unique visual identity for the spot. Schedule: "Ten days of shooting, four weeks of artistic and technical research and five weeks of production."

records.title: TNT "THE PEOPLE NETWORK"
records.description: PostPanic director Mischa Rozema in Amsterdam: "There was just no way to turn a script like this down, even though it had 'IMPOSSIBLE' written all over it. The complexity, the size, the craziness. Maybe that's what really pulled me in to this. I just loved stepping into the unknown and finding out how we could make this work. "The biggest challenge was how to avoid the VFX becoming the focus of the TVC. PostPanic is set up differently than most production companies because we have our own in-house post production team which works instinctively with the directors. "The temptation would have been to apply all that specialised knowledge and make this into a VFX fest but actually we threw out a lot of VFX when we started the project. "We decided to really push what could be achieved in camera by actually creating a full size human truck on the set. It worked by having a huge, truck-sized, metal rig that could be pulled by an actual truck. "We then filled it with an incredible Czech stunt team (famous for big Hollywood blockbusters) that had been rehearsing for weeks and gave the whole project a realistic approach. "To be honest in the end, we used more VFX in the backgrounds (creating a non-existing airport, alpine road-tunnels and cities) than on the actual vehicles where you'd expect them." Ivor Goldberg, head of post and creative partner at PostPanic: "Of all the challenges on this project (which were numerous) two were clear winners. First was creating CG humans to go alongside real humans in the same shot. Everyone is an expert and a critic on what a human should look like – there is nowhere to hide. "Secondly, it was always the intention to shoot as much as possible in camera (mostly because of the problems of the first challenge). Logistically this became undoable. "In the end we had to shoot not only multiple takes but also multiple takes in multiple locations and stitch these all together to create one good image that we could then embellish with CG. Typically in one shot there could be up to 10 elements shot at three or four different locations." Annejes van Liempd, PostPanic executive producer: "Our choice of using real people for this rather than CG humans dictated the nature of the shoot making it an extremely technical one both in pre-production and during actual filming. "We had so many variables which had to work together and fit perfectly for multiple passes on most of the shots. This resulted in agonisingly time-consuming days, almost two weeks away filming but the stunt team kept us all laughing. We really enjoyed working with the whole Czech crew (via Savage) - they were amazing." Ivor Goldberg: "I take enormous pride in this team here at PostPanic. They are true all-round artists. In an industry where pipelines and workflows can be so rigid and constricting I love that they, as individuals, can not only undertake such a wide variety of disciplines from matte painting to animating and compositing but still get genuine pleasure from the creative and technical process. "It is this which I feel is quite rare in the industry and really allows us to produce such quality in such short turnarounds without people running out the door in terror never to be seen again." Schedule: three months.

records.title: FIRST DIRECT "LITTLE FRILL" (Extended version)
records.description: Jon Park, VFX supervisor at MPC in London: "The brief was to stick to the anatomical constraints of a frill-necked lizard but creatively make him behave like a human being trapped in a lizard's body. The spot was shot on 35mm Kodak film, which is quite rare in these digital times. "The main creative challenge was to raise the bar on the previous first direct 'Platypus' commercials. Secondly, our Little Frill character spends all his time standing upright, which a real lizard wouldn't do. "The team manipulated his body to stand in a human position; referencing footage of comedian Seann Walsh holding a giant phone recorded during his voiceover. It then became a balancing act between human and lizard performances for the animators. "The main technical challenge was that the lizard has very small arms and animating them to make human gestures made him look pretty awkward but without changing his body shape there was no escaping this. "So we decided to embrace the fact he has tiny little arms (like Rex in 'Toy Story') and made the most of it by making him gesticulate a lot, which makes him look pretty funny. "Also, the opening shot was difficult as it is an extreme close-up of the DJ-ing tarsier's eyes. Creating 3D realistic eyes is just about the hardest thing to do, so a lot of time was spent getting them to look just right." Schedule: 2 1/2 months.

records.title: OREO "REPLAY" Extended version
records.description: Hue&Cry creative director Magnus Hierta in Richmond, Virginia: "The client brief was simple and direct. It consisted of a song and lyrics paired with a set of simple visual guidelines. The song is based around a simple question asking: 'Wonder if I gave an Oreo to someone, would it give them an optimistic outlook?' "The visual guidelines spoke of bold vibrant colors, simple graphic uncluttered space, and a focus on impactful typography. In fact, they wanted the typography to be see-and-say in the fashion of a karaoke video. Very fun indeed! "The creative challenge was fairly straightforward: Design a spot that fit into the bold, clean look of the new Wonderfilled campaign. We were tasked with creating a spot based around typography with supporting elements and design vignettes that worked in support of the type. "And it had to bridge the high school theme of the lyrics with the hip-hop music track aesthetics into an aesthetic appealing to everyone, from kids to moms (OREO's core buyer). Oh, and of course it needed to be watchable again and again. "The project had an extremely tight three-week timeline and an approved look that included a lot of cel animation. Needless to say, this combination is not the most forgiving! "So we approached it systematically. We created scenes that utilized a lot of repeated elements which created a graphic, grid-like quality. This allowed us to minimize the amount of cel animation needed so we could focus our animators on some of the bigger key elements. "For the typography we built a Cinema 4D rig that allowed us to iterate type changes quickly. We rendered them with the Sketch and Toon shading plug-in for the cel animated look. That output was paired with standard render passes using clamped ambient occlusion maps to create natural shading to the Toon rendered lines. It did the trick just right." Schedule: "We had a three week production schedule to deliver :15, :30 and :45 second spots!"

records.title: SNICKERS "BRADY BUNCH"
records.description: Seamless and surprisingly extensive VFX from The Mill for the Snickers Super Bowl spot starring Danny Trejo as Marcia Brady and Steve Buscemi as Jan. Visual effects supervisor Nick Tanner at The Mill, New York: "2D lead artist Nathan Kane worked with the team to build a pre-vis to try and figure out the spatial representation of that old Brady Bunch set. "Then, on the shoot day the whole set was replicated as closely as possible to the original to give Danny Trejo and Steve Buscemi an environment grounded in reality, with furniture they could interact with. This allowed for the axe throwing improvisation and Steve's tantrum at the top of the steps to occur. "The approach to filming was an intensive part of the final visual effects. We needed to capture 180 degrees of the stand-ins' faces and place Danny and Steve in the Brady living room. "We made sure the stand-in actors were fixed in place to minimize their movements, and set up five witness cameras on all sides to capture their performance from every angle. "Their faces were then tracked onto CG geometry of the original characters' faces. The team was cautious about tracking with the decades old footage that included a high level of artifacts and grain. "The body doubles (cast for their mouth, chin and lip features and filmed against greenscreen) would say the lines and this footage was tracked and transplanted onto the original footage of Florence Henderson as Mrs. Brady and Robert Reed as Mr. Brady. But the actual voice of Henderson heard in the spot was a character voiceover artist. "Finally, grain and texture was added to each shot, giving it the vintage treatment to fit in with the rest of the footage. "Even though the team hasn't seen either actor in many commercials, they knew Steve Buscemi would be the perfect person to convey the internal angst of Jan. He was interested as soon we reached out. "Danny Trejo took his turn as Marcia Brady extremely seriously during filming. Watching Danny angrily yell at Mr. and Mrs. Brady was a treat."

records.title: LEGOLAND "AWESOME AWAITS"
records.description: Mill+ director Russell Tickner in London: "Collaborating closely with the agency creative team, all of the various VFX specialists worked together from the outset, involved in every element from the pre-production, storyboarding and character design, to the 'bricking' animation tools developed specifically for this job. Joint head of 3D at The Mill, Dave Fleet: "Firstly, our characters were modeled as polygonal meshes. These were then rigged and animated, then passed from Maya to Houdini using Mill+'s custom caching format. "At this point the animators would also export what we refer to as a 'call sheet'. This is basically a live list of ingredients that go into each scene. Russell and the animators were regularly changing characters, so it was vital to make this as easy as possible so the FX and lighting teams were always up to date. "We then started the process of turning the animated characters into bricks, by creating our own plugin aptly named Bricker. Bricker was seamlessly integrated into our existing pipeline and automatically picked up animation updates and knew when new characters got added or removed from a shot. "As LEGO bricks come in all different shapes and sizes we built sliders within the tool so the artist could decide which bricks were used and ultimately how the character was built. "The Pirate ship had the most, at around three million individual LEGO bricks, not including the huge wave it was riding. Bricker included many other optimization features like camera culling and hollowing out the characters to save on bricks and to speed up the whole workflow. "The bricked characters were then passed onto our lighting team as a huge point cloud, each point representing the location and color of a brick. This allowed our lighting scenes to be very lightweight as the LEGO bricks themselves are only created at render time using Arnold's powerful instancing system." Schedule: "Eight months from initial concept images to the final spot."

records.title: BGH "THE CHASE"
records.description: Nicolas Cantarelli, CGI director at Laposta in Buenos Aires: "The client wanted to show a new smartphone with a smart idea and wanted to make it in a fantastic and surreal way. "Directed by Jonathan Gurvit, the spot focuses on the speed of the red 'play' bar trying to catch up to the grey 'download' bar and extends as a metaphor showing us how dramatic slow downloads could be. "At the beginning we had to choose which actions we wanted to show, so we had to draw lot of ideas from the agency and from ourselves. The selection process was tough. Lot of good ideas were thrown in the trash. We especially loved one with a Chinese dragon chasing a Samurai. Maybe we have to wait for a second part of this campaign to see it. "Our main challenge was to design and create all of the CGI environments because the only thing they could shoot was the actors and extras running in the studio. "It was really difficult to understand how the bees fly to make them look real but technical at the same time. The smoke of the train was another issue we had to take care of, because we had to simulate lots of frames to have it in slow motion. "After finding the correct hardware to cache all that, we managed to process all that data to generate the long and realistic smoke effects. "During pre-production we decided the best way to shoot this spot would be in a dark place to emphasize this dramatic staging. At compositing we had to rotoscope all the characters on all the shots. "We knew this would be artist-intensive, and we would have to use lot of time to make all the masks to composite the backgrounds but with this method we achieved a much better comp." Schedule: two months.

records.title: HOVIS GOOD INSIDE "STUCK"
records.description: MPC head of 3D Anthony Bloor in London: "To get the right feeling for the story Johnny wanted to tell, we needed to have full control of the way the brick wall was built, what elements were made of and how they behave. "The treatment gave us a good initial idea of how things should look, but it was important to be able to iterate fast and make quick reviews to fit into the agency's and director's vision. "To complete the project quickly and efficiently a procedural modeling and animation system was written to build and animate the walls. With this system the artists had the ability to dial the parameters and have all the elements automatically placed and modeled with physical accuracy. This allowed for great creative control and artistic fine tuning to achieve the director's vision for each shot. "Some of the elements – bricks, breeze blocks, plasterboard, studs, tiles and even 1980s style wallpaper – frenetically build behind the leading edge of the walls automatically responding to the character of the wall. "Thousands of high-detail models populate the house as it builds through the environment, but also much of the environment was enhanced too with everything from the sky to the grass replaced in several shots. "The walls had various moods throughout. At first it was able to build quickly and straight, but as the kids tried to trick it, the walls start to twist and turn getting less perfect and building with more and more random items. "Towards the end it's already wobbling ready to fall over before the final destruction. We also simulate some light dust which helped to add realism without excessively covering the action."

records.title: THE FEEL GOOD BAKERY "FEEL GOOD FILM"
records.campaign_title: THE FEEL GOOD BAKERY "FEEL GOOD FILM"
records.description: Stephen Simmonds, creative director of weareseventeen, in London: "When we met Andy from Regenerate UK and found out about The Feel Good Bakery and the great work they do, we immediately wanted to use our skills to help get more awareness for the charity. There wasn't a brief as such; we just wanted to work with Andy and help in any way we could to raise awareness of his great organization. "Originally Andy was looking for more of a traditional 'explainer' to inform viewers of what the Feel Good Bakery does. We thought it might be a good idea to start our relationship by just simply spreading a little of the 'Feel Good'. "So the challenge was coming up with an idea that touched on what happens at the Feel Good Bakery, make people feel good about it and not come across as too worthy. "Originally we set out to do this in 2D which fit nicely with the feel we were going for. However, it soon became obvious that if we approached the animation in a 3D sense we would have a lot more flexibility with what we could do. So we needed to recreate the illustrative look and feel we had created in 2D in 3D. Ultimately this was that difficult but we had to change the way we were working and approach things from a slightly different angle. "If you ever get the chance to work with a charity you believe in, do it! It makes you feel great to think that the job you love doing will actually do some good for real people that need it. It makes a real change to the commercial world we are all too familiar with." Schedule: three months.

records.title: CREATIVE CLOSETS "ADVANCED STATE OF MIND"
records.description: Christopher Vulpi, co-founder and executive producer at Trizz in Düsseldorf, Germany: "The client referenced two of our existing projects (Nika and Armani) and asked us to make a concept where the product is formed in a dream-like way. "This project involved everything in 3D, so we had to not only replicate the product's mechanics, but also every element that would appear. We researched and casted for everything from surfaces, LEDs lights, clothes, interior decor, architecture to plants on the floor. "Creating everything in 3D means that the client has to clearly understand our vision in steps - from mood boards to style frames to render tests and pre-vis - we make sure they see everything we see, and have a chance to ask questions before going on to the next step. "It's our policy not to scare clients with technology, so we don't talk tech, but rather we play show and tell and take their comments into the work right away. "We use pencils. A photocopier. And a creative robot, named Oriol-One-Thousand. Only kidding. We shoot live-action on Alexa, edited in FCP, animated in Maya, rendered in V-Ray, some elements in Reflow, and we comp on our 2D and Smoke and color grade on our DaVinci."

records.title: MORTON SALT "NEIGHBORS" FOR ICE MELT & SAFE T-PET
records.campaign_title: MORTON SALT "NEIGHBORS" FOR ICE MELT & SAFE T-PET
records.description: Director Marc Craste at Studio AKA in London: "The brief was to create a heartwarming story with the feel of a classic cartoon short. The story needed to convey the dogs' friendship and the desperation they feel at being forced apart. That Morton Salt should be the catalyst for reuniting them was the key beat that had to be absolutely clear. "As always, the main challenge comes down to telling the story in the most effective way possible within the time frame. There were a lot of lovely ideas built around the dogs' friendship in the original script that we had to jettison in the interest of getting the important beats of the story across. "That's always hard. We were also keen to create something reminiscent of golden age cartoons, but without slavishly adhering to the style or becoming too nostalgic about it. So we took elements of the look and the storytelling of that era but kept the visuals crisp and contemporary. "The rigging of the dogs was a challenge. A tight schedule meant moving the production into animation early on, leaving little time to test the rigs – which included finding one solution to work for both bulldog and fox terrier. In addition, all CG elements had to be designed to incorporate the final 2D look, including hand-drawn linework." Schedule: three months.

records.title: SLACK TEAMS DO AMAZING THINGS "ANIMALS"
records.description: Adam Foulkes and Alan Smith, directors at Nexus Productions in London: "The client was very keen to show Slack as a collaborative messaging tool, so that's where the idea of an unlikely team being able to communicate smoothly came about. And what is more unlikely than a random collection of animals? "Slack is a new product so there was an obvious need to explain what it is and what makes it different from other messaging apps. But it was very important that this did not turn into the dreaded product demonstration video. "There were all kinds of features they wanted to highlight such as uploading and downloading files, searching in a specific Slack channel and staying in touch with the team while being out of the office, so we tried to seamlessly weave all these into the story. "Whenever you create a new universe of characters you have to invent all the rules to go with it. Which animals and in what roles, do they wear clothes, can they speak, do they want to eat each other, how can a goat type? "All of these questions had to be answered and it seemed that everyone had a different opinion. But mostly you go on your gut instincts on what makes you laugh. "If there's ever been a lion and prawn on screen together before we can't think of it, and it just seems funny that they have to queue up to use the photocopier. "The other main challenge was to give them a task to complete, and after much debate about the size and nature of this task the client came up with the idea of the drone umbrella. We could then tell this story by showing the way the team use Slack to communicate their ideas to each other. "We considered many techniques but finally decided on portraying recognizably realistic settings. This gave us an enjoyable oddness, seeing our animals living alongside humans and inhabiting the same world as our own. "It also established a very matter of fact documentary performance style, almost as if we filmed real office workers and then turned them into animals. It was more 'The Office' than 'Madagascar'. "The main challenge with any photo-realistic project is believability, so getting the fur renders to react with the practical lighting and making sure the animated characters interact correctly with real props was paramount. "We first filmed real people acting out each scene to give us a sense of how the animals would behave and what sort of difficulties they would encounter as they moved around the office. We could also work out what the camera had to do. For instance, filming focus pulls in camera really helped merge the characters into the scenes during the composite."

records.title: THE ROAD TO RIO "I AM TEAM GB"
records.campaign_title: THE ROAD TO RIO "I AM TEAM GB"
records.description: Creative director Mike Moloney at Art&Graft in London: "We were tasked with creating an integrated campaign comprising a set of charming animated commercials and promos, point of sale and out of home collateral for The National Lottery and ITV's support of Team GB at the Rio 2016 Olympic Games. "Working in collaboration with ITN Productions, ITV Creative and ITV AdVentures we directed, designed and produced a range of items which aim to inspire and represent the 'togetherness' that each Olympic Games brings to the nation; that we're all joined together as we get behind our athletes. "We wanted to create the epic, cinematic scenes synonymous with an Olympics launch, yet also introduce a warmth and charm that is sometimes missing when representing our heroic athletic superstars. "The 'Road to Rio' focuses on the story of Camelot being a key funder of Team GB: supporting over 1,300 athletes on their Roads to Rio; allowing them to train full time and have the best coaching, facilities and medical support in the world. "Every National lottery ticket and Scratchcard sold across the nation helps contribute to the over £80 million per year that goes to Team GB. As such, the film focuses on a transformative flock of tickets as they journey throughout the day to each corner of the UK – from the shores of Loch Lomond to the Angel of the North and Giant's Causeway, magically transforming the equipment and kit of the heroic training athletes it encounters. "We wanted to create cinematic, sweeping landscapes and 3D character animation combined with a rich illustrative approach to create a memorable series of animated films and print which capture the true celebratory spirit and humanity of the Olympic Games. "Influenced by the paintings of Norman Wilkinson - his beautiful representations of British landscapes and sense of four seasons in one day - we sought to incorporate stunning lighting and a warm color palette into the design of the environments. "We wanted the tickets to feel magical and mischievous as they spring to life in the morning sunlight then, once they join together in a flock, to feel graceful and elegant as they sweep through the air and transform our Team GB athletes."

records.title: AMERICAN HORROR STORY ANTHOLOGY
records.description: Kasper Verweij, director and founder at ONESIZE in Amsterdam: "FX was very clear in what they wanted for this promo and why they wanted us to use the key art of previous seasons: They wanted to leave the viewer guessing what the final season was going to be about, creating buzz amongst American Horror Story fans. "The main focus for this promo was to reacquaint the viewer with the memorable marketing in AHS. For the pitch we set out to create a seamless ride through all the previous seasons, without adding any new design element to tie them together, so all elements used are derived from the key art posters. "Since this is in the horror genre, we felt we needed to have a retracting motion in the camera, symbolizing running away. "The gimp trying to grab the camera sets off this backward pull. To keep the stylistic feel of the prints, we decided to create everything in CG, even the black figure in the first scene. This way we had full control over both camera and animation. "Second creative choice we had to make was the way we would go from one to the other scene, while keeping it completely seamless. All of the scenes had one thing in common: they all feature characters. Going through the mouths of these characters felt like the way to go. "Other elements that could tie the scenes together were specific materials. Combining this led us to go through either the mouth or by tying textures together from one scene to the other. "To test if this approach was going to work, and to convince FX of this treatment, we created an animatic showing most of the elements and the transition we wanted to go for. Subtle details like the crying of the nun's eyes and life-like animation of characters like the gimp and the snake, would make this spot more than just a simple pull through five pieces of key art. Animating the fabric and the sky would only add to this feeling. "To really craft this sequence, the team at ONESIZE employed a series of different techniques, including 3D, camera mapping, modeling and animation." Schedule: one month.

records.title: HATSU "BETTER TOGETHER", "HELLO! HATSU"
records.description: Pablo Alfieri, founder and director at Playful in Buenos Aires: "The brief has been totally open since the beginning of our relationship with Hatsu, a Colombian tea brand only five years old but with a big potential in a new and increasing market of healthy drinks around the world. "They wanted consumers and future clients to feel the soul of the product. So we played on the idea of 'Hatsu meets Memphis Milano' an excuse to travel between different sets and the nine bottles of tea showing the exotic and fresh spirit of Hatsu. "For Hatsu 'Better Together' the creative challenge was to produce it in only one month with two days of shooting. Everything was made and approved for the client in only 12 days. "For Becho & Mab, the great animators of the spot, the technical challenge was how to animate the bottles at the pack shot, so they created an awesome mechanism to make them go up and down fluidly. "With the 'Hello Hatsu!' spot, we couldn't afford a real handcrafted spot, so we ventured into realistic 3D animation with fancy, exotic and colorful sets. "For 'Hello Hatsu!' we used C4D and Nuke. For 'Hatsu Better Together' we used C4D for the set design, shot with an Alexa for live action, and the stop-motion was made with a pair of Canon 5Ds." Schedule: "'Hello Hatsu!': six weeks total: two for design, three for animation, one for rendering and post production. Hatsu 'Better Together': One month total: two weeks for design, two weeks for post-production."

records.title: AIR MAX '17
records.description: ManvsMachine creative director, Adam Rowe in Los Angeles: "Our brief was to conceive and produce the campaign creative for the Nike Air Max '17 with the core callouts being comfort and breathability. "The main creative challenge was trying to get buy-in to the edit style and audio approach. We had something in our minds that was tricky to storyboard and turn into an animatic without going ahead and creating the final piece. "Thankfully, Nike trusted us and allowed us the freedom to flesh out the concept enough to push it through. "The trickiest aspect of the project was one of quantity. Our aim was to visually overload the viewer with as many metaphors as possible. The catch-22 was that we had to produce a plethora of shots, many of which were completely different from one another. "In order to make this more manageable, we had planned to work on each scene for slightly less time than we usually would - purely due to the fact that each would be on screen for such a short amount of time – but, true to form, we ended up crafting every tiny detail to the nth degree on twice as many shots as normal. "With the edit being comprised of so many different scenes, each designer used various combinations of software packages. Our main tools of choice were Cinema 4D, Houdini, Maya, V-Ray, Redshift, Adobe Creative Cloud and ZBrush. "Perhaps noteworthy is that the shot of the shoe sucking into a fabric sphere was created as a small motion test in the first week of the project. It made the final cut without any simulation tweaks at all." Schedule: "It's tricky with this project to put a time stamp on the production as there wasn't a definitive split between creative development and production. All in all it was somewhere in the region of two months."

records.title: BBC "EVERY ELEMENT OF WONDER"
records.description: Flink creative lead Daniel Balzer in Hamburg, Germany: "This 50-second ad brings together 39 of the BBC's learning titles [across TV, radio, digital and social media] into one carefully crafted movie, combining a large variety of subjects and content into one visually connected piece. "'Every Element of Wonder', is a celebration of learning built on a slick reimagining of Tom Lehrer's 1959 periodic table song, 'The Elements', in which BBC titles replace the scientific elements. "The titles and content whirl together and transform into a cubical shape, and thus retaining its visual connection to the BBC periodic table from the start to the end of the film. "In the ad's whirling culmination, the titles come together in their own table to form 'Every element of wonder available across the BBC'. "The song was brought to life by the impressive lyrical talents of Golden Globe award-winning actress Olivia Coleman, who mastered her recital of all 39 BBC titles! "We used a combination of fully CG generated content, footage and motion design elements to illustrate the learning content available across BBC's factual TV and radio output, its digital resources and learning initiatives, highlighting shows from Brian Cox's 'Forces of Nature' to 'The Infinite Monkey Cage.'"

records.title: VERNER PANTON PANTHELLA MINI
records.description: Thomas Bay, executive producer and partner at Frame in Copenhagen, Denmark: "The client Louis Poulsen showed us some images from an exhibition Danish designer Verner Panton did in 1998, just prior to his death. "They thought it would be great to use that exhibition as a main inspiration for the spot and as we are huge fans of Panton, we were totally on board with that. "There were two key challenges. One thing was to make a design that was light and contemporary while still having a clear reference to the aesthetics of Verner Panton. "In the first set of style frames, we did have color combinations that were closer to some of his original ones for instance, but the client wanted to give it a more modern look. And I think it became more fresh and more its own thing actually, which I like. "The second challenge was to create the edit. It had to have the right pace, present all the lamps in all their colors, have the right balance between abstract and product shots and have a meaningful transition from shot to shot. That took a lot of feedback sessions and fiddling around to get that right. "The biggest technical issue was the light emission in Octane, because it gave a lot of noise, so we had to render out with a lot more samples than if the lamps had been turned off." Schedule: "We had one month from our first meeting with the client. So it was pretty tight. With one guy on it from start to finish, and another couple of guys on for three weeks."

records.title: TURBOTAX: "HUMPTY FALL"
records.description: James Allen, shoot supervisor and 2D lead artist at The Mill LA: "Our job was to aid in Wieden+Kennedy's retelling of a classic story by creating a photo-real character with a real person's face and an oversized model of an egg. "Our main creative challenge was to create Humpty in three distinct stages of repair. The first stage takes place immediately after Humpty falls off the wall: shell, egg yolk, eyes and mouth scattered in a mess on the ground. "The second stage sees the aftermath of the Kingsmen's unsuccessful attempt to put him back together. In the final stage, Humpty's in the hospital. "Legacy built a fantastic practical oversized egg which we augmented and manipulated to illustrate Humpty's painful road to recovery. "One of our primary technical challenges was marrying a solid egg with a real, moving face as it spoke. It took considerable stabilizing and morphing to achieve a seamless composite. "We shot at multiple locations in LA over a period of four days last November and finished the spots in January. Schedule: six months.

records.title: OPPO "R11"
records.description: Director SOMEI in Shanghai: "OPPO asked me to make a new ID video for their newly released R11 mobile phone as we have worked together for four years. "The brief is very simple. They want to keep the color and fashion tone I have already built for them, and hope to see some new breakthroughs. "And they give me three or four selling points like the curve of back shell, dual camera, and the two-line design of the antenna. No other limits, I just play around with anything I want to try. "I think the most challenging part is to make design breakthroughs based on the existing style. I really hope the audience can get some freshness from the video and I was stuck for a really long time, until two days before the deadline for conception. "I saw a video called 'Unsatisfying' and I really liked it because it had a little story in every scene. It's more than just visual, there was some psychological chemical reaction happening. Then I decide to put the selling points into different scenes and design some little stories, like the unexpected moments. "And then I found there should be something that can trigger the unexpected moment, so I put a hand in the video. "The concept was completed in seven days and then I made the animatic (most of the animation) in another seven days, and then it took three-four days to approve it. "Then I did the lighting and pondering the design; it took 15 days to make the first version, and another 10 days to do some adjustments and changes according to the comments from client. "One interesting thing is that you will not see any blue color in OPPO's commercials, because blue is the main color of the competition's brand. OPPO's color is green, so as the result even the sky is green in this video."

records.title: THREE "GO ROAM"
records.description: Lead 3D artist Alex Hammond at The Mill in London: "Being a full CG job, it was essential to define the look of the characters and environment in the early stages. "Working closely with director The Perlorian Brothers, we defined key references of how our world should look and produced multiple concepts which helped to show the progression of how surreal our landscape would become. "Early animation tests allowed us to develop how our bizarre character – a giraffamingo would behave. "It had to be 'sassy and confident' which meant our animators looked at a lot of music video references, largely by Beyoncé!"

records.title: SKY SPORTS "START THE SEASON"
records.description: The Mill joint head of 3D Michael Chapman: "The main challenge of this job was to bring a sense of drama to the iconic sporting locations through the butterfly motif. "The Mill's VFX team worked on a total of 73 shots, producing over five million butterflies for the larger stadium shots. They also carried out extensive matte painting work to enhance the stadium scenes, crafting some of the stadiums entirely in CG. "The team meticulously modeled six species of butterflies taken from real life references to create the swarms. "On set, we shot numerous butterflies to study how they behaved and reacted to the many different lighting conditions which we filmed in. "We based our shading and lighting on these references, tweaking the patterns of each species of butterfly to suit the environments so their presence felt tangible. "We knew the animation of these creatures was going to be integral to the whole piece so we focused on creating flap cycles from the reference we had captured on set and from other nature documentaries. "We then used these animations to drive simulations for the large-scale shots, making sure each individual butterfly had realistic movement. We also hand-animated the foreground butterflies in each shot to give us precise control over their position and movement. "We used Maya to build and animate the butterflies, we simulated the large flocks in Houdini and then we rendered through our in-house render procedural in Arnold within Maya."

records.title: CEREBOS "SNOW"
records.description: Executive producer Nina Pfeiffer at Tulips and Chimneys in Cape Town, South Africa: "We received a detailed script from FCB Durban about Mpho, a little girl dreaming of snow in a hot arid place. "Her dreams become a reality when her parents and grandma conspire to make her dreams come true by sprinkling salt from above the rooftop of her bedroom window. "Since we needed to fit the story into 30 seconds we had to take these beautiful ideas and rework them to develop the individual personalities of the characters and the narrative in such a way that the core idea came through in the best way possible. "We decided to set the story in the Karoo as it's one of the most arid but also most interesting regions of South Africa. We felt that the vast open spaces would support the futility of our lead character's dream. "We then decided she should be living with her grandma and grandpa rather than her parents which allowed us to eliminate one of the characters in the original script and still make the situation believable as a fair number of children in SA are bought up by their grandparents for various reasons. "This allowed us to spend a little more time on her grandparents and focusing on their personalities. We then looked at the different actions that Mpho could perform in each shot making it clear that she was dreaming of snow since we would have no narration over the story. "This resulted in the fun little skits she plays out in each shot: making snow angels, riding a makeshift sleigh and dreamily staring into a snow globe. "We also ensured that Gramps was constantly tinkering on something in the background so when the fantastic pulley system is revealed in the end it's clear he's been supportive of Mpho all along. "Creatively this project really was a dream; we had a great team onboard from the client to the agency to the creative team. We can honestly say it was one of the smoothest most pleasant productions we've ever worked on. Executive producers Marc Bloch and Marco Raposo de Barbosaat at Black Ginger: "For us the biggest challenge was to translate the 2D illustrations into 3D characters and bring them to life. There was a lot of back and forth getting Mpho just right. "We wanted the spot to feel like it's taking part throughout the course of a day so lighting was going to play a vital role from the beginning. The DOP Johan Horjus was fantastic at managing this. Here are a few technical challenges and solutions he faced: "The Flickering light from the TV was created by sliding 3 cm x 3 cm blue and diffuser gels between the light hidden behind the TV, about 40 times, without moving anything else. "A 30 kg light with a camera lens was rigged 2 m up looking down, then the spot of light was reduced to shine on an area of 4 cm, only to create more definition on the stove in the kitchen. "All the long traveling shots over the landscape were shot upside-down so that we get get closer to the ground. "The warm side light on the rope and gears that grandpa build was a slither of light about 2 cm and masked off the wall with black tinfoil of about 1 cm. Only to separate it from the wall and to add some texture. "The bedside light was created from a 360 LED light. A rod that was attached to the column of the light that continued all the way down to underneath the set. This is where I turned/rotated the bedside light every second frame by hand, the increments were as small as I could possible move, about 120 times. "The inspiration of the little round bushes decorating the Karoo landscape came from a hike we did near Kalk Bay. We came across an extraordinary patch of rust-colored moss that looked just like miniature Karoo bushes and kept that in mind when briefing the concept artists "Set decorating for the outside shots was a lot of fun, the textured ground was a mixture of sand, tiny pebbles and tea! "We then added hundreds of tiny sprigs of rosemary that lead up to the larger bushes that were created with moss died different colors. "We grouped various elements together and then gently made them bleed into the other elements to create arrangements that appeared true to nature even though our plant designs were stylised. "A lot of thought went into the shape of our characters ...Mpho is shaped like an upside down triangle, her cuteness factor largely comes from her having such a big head in relation to her body and her tiny feet. "Her grandma on the other hand is bell shaped, completely the opposite or rather the reverse of Mpho. Her shape is an ode to her larger than life personality. She is definitely the matriarch of the family. "Gramps on the other hand is a skinny bean of a man. He takes up very little space in the house and is quiet and unassuming. However he observes everything so closely, and in the end it's his patient tinkering and exquisite mind that brings so much joy to Mpho and Grandma. "Mpho's sidekicks are three chickens that ended up stealing the show! We absolutely love them and are hoping we have the opportunity to developed their stories further down the line. "We enjoyed coming up with touches for the set that were truly South African: pumpkins drying out on the red roof a Karoo farm house; old ginger beer bottles typically found in old farmsteads; a coat hanger being used as the TV aerial. "We took great care in the design and ageing of the 1950's couch in the lounge. It's quite obviously been sat on for years, and grandma carefully crocheted the doilies to prevent greasy hair staining the couch. It's these tiny touches that make the spot so special." Schedule: Eight weeks pre-production, 10 days shooting and 10 weeks post production.

records.title: VOLKSWAGEN "BORN CONFIDENT"
records.description: Carsten Keller, 3D creative director at MPC: "We needed to create a baby ram with life-like proportions, staying true to physical anatomy. To make him feel real, subtlety was key. "Push the animation and acting too hard and you instantly lose believability – the emotion and storytelling in 'Born Confident' comes from our little hero's elegant and confident posing, with no need for buffed-up, oversized muscles. "Using innovative in-house software developed for photo-real creature work, MPC's artists crafted the photo-real character harnessing the expertise and learnings of our 'Life' team from across the studio, including the Jungle Book team in MPC Film."

records.title: PLAYSTATION VR SKYRIM "CLAWS"
records.description: Nirad "Bugs" Russell (senior producer), Gregory Gangemi (CG lead) and Nathan Kane (shoot/VFX supervisor) at The Mill in New York: GG: "The brief was to create an epic spot that really conveyed the feeling of being thrown into the VR world of Skyrim. We interpreted that as an opportunity to push the look and feel of the Skyrim world for the new generation of VR gamers." NK: "Getting the scale of the Dragon to feel right was definitely the biggest challenge of this job. We spent a lot of time in animation to make sure the dragon felt like it had enough weight. "We also created a lot of environmental effects that added to the weight of the dragon, like the snow interaction on impact and subtlety of wind created by the dragon's wings. "The fire created by the dragon was also an extremely challenging effect to pull off. After discussing it with the director Wayne McClammy, we all agreed that we needed to capture something in camera. "We did extensive tests with different flame throwers to give us the desired look of the fire. The in-camera fire would act as the main body of the effect, but we also combined CG fire for extra shape and intensity." BR: "We received assets about a month before the shoot to get ourselves ready for the scale of the dragon. The production included two 20-hour shoot days." GG: "Our 3D pipeline is Maya-Arnold based, with sculpting in ZBrush and effects done in Houdini. Comping was done in Nuke and matte painting in Photoshop. "One interesting note was that at the start of the job, Autodesk was in-house working on their new effects tools for Maya. Todd Akita helped them to work out some kinks by using some of the Skyrim shots as test cases."

records.title: EDF "THE RACE"
records.description: Guillaume Marien, owner and VFX EP at Mathematic in Paris: "This was a great opportunity as well as a great challenge for us, a full 3D film that is both dynamic and at the same time has cinematographic elegance. "The complexity of the challenge was due to the necessity to design and create realistic and charismatic characters. The environments during the game sequence were 100 percent developed in CGI due to the vast camera movements. "Although the majority of the work was conducted through our Paris office this was also our first experience to test out our VFX pipeline capacity with our new office in Montreal. Fingers crossed for a sequel."

records.title: HENDRICK'S GIN "ESCAPE"
records.description: Director Ree Treweek: "We have long been admirers of the Hendrick's Gin aesthetic. Its Victoriana surrealism is so aligned with our style that you can imagine our delight when we were approached by agency Quaker City Mercantile to create an animated spot. "We loved the idea that the architecture itself reflects the theme of the spot, and is alive and changing . "Our commuters' office block works like an old-fashioned clock hand, while the homes of our lead characters resemble an alligator and a swordfish. "We played with scale within the environments and built on the idea that things are constantly changing, from the lighting to the sky tones." "Tulips and Chimneys created the layered illustrated artwork in Photoshop then animated and composited in After Effects adding grain, vignettes, dust, scratches, film burn, and light leaks associated with old film stock."

records.title: L&C "GLIDE"
records.description: The newly unified Paris studios of MPC Advertising and Mikros handle the feathery creature craft in this cheeky and hard-to-ignore full-CG spot directed by Future Deluxe for UK mortgage brokers L&C through agency Fold7.

records.title: "ULTRABOOST X PARLEY"
records.description: Taylor Shortall, social media coordinator at Psyop in Los Angeles: "It's not often you get to create a project that can make a positive impact on the world. "This spot highlights Adidas' new UltraBOOST PARLEY shoes, the latest in their collaboration with Parley for the Oceans. Each pair of shoes prevents approximately 11 plastic bottles from entering our oceans. "The original brief was to create a fairly straightforward plastic-to-thread-to-shoe story, which was to play out on the surface of the shoe. "Although we liked the idea, we felt that the story deserved a more indepth treatment that also lined up with their wider social media-inspired campaign. "We wanted to get across the community spirit/effort that was making it possible for consumers to help stop plastic waste from entering our oceans and the mixed media approach felt right for that. "We went a little off brief with our treatment, but the guys at TBWA and Adidas supported our vision fully. "The fiber is not only the actual production process, from collected bottle to shoe, but it is also very metaphorical: the thread that connects everything. It shows how every action has a consequence and how the universe is connected – we can't isolate one thing from another. "Balancing the number of different styles was a challenge, but also a big reason why we were into the project as it gave us a chance to mix the best of Golden Wolf and Psyop into one piece." Jonah Friedman, technical director at Psyop: "We needed to make hundreds of these, CG embroidered patches to animate in stop motion, so we had to be very efficient. "Our solution was a new system, called the Patchtwiner, a system and toolbox for artists to turn 2D animation into properly 'entwined' patches. "Every frame of our animation looks as though an artist stitched a bespoke patch, creating contours and laying down stitches to represent the image in the best way possible. "Stop motion results in imperfections, and we recreated those for ourselves. The patches are differently deformed on every frame, as if they were sewn to a piece of fabric that wouldn't sit still. The light jitters on every frame, and the effect is complete." Psyop founder Marco Spier: "This project is very close to my heart. I got involved with Parley for the Oceans from the very beginning and having the opportunity to help spread the message together with Adidas and TBWACHIATDAY has been a great honor. "This is bigger than us. This is about survival. Psyop has helped a lot of brands to get their message out, so now it's time for us the make the ocean our biggest client." Schedule: 10 weeks.

records.title: BANKWEST "HALO"
records.description: Entertainment and clarity merge perfectly in this vibrant and upbeat :30 from Buck's Sydney studio introducing the Halo ring for Bankwest which allows you to fist-bump the payment terminal to complete your transaction. Jordan Howes, producer at Buck in Sydney, Australia: "We were asked to create a cast of characters and series of spots for Bankwest. Each spot focuses on a different product or service and is told through light-hearted character-driven stories. "The main challenge was meeting print deadlines which came well before the film delivery. We had to pose characters without their rigs and fasttrack the character design and look dev. "The spots have been broadcast on television in Australia and on large outdoor screens in major cities. The print campaign has been rolled out across Australia as well as being used in Bankwest branches."

records.title: HABITO "HELL OR HABITO"
records.description: Andy Baker, director at Strange Beast in London: "Showing just how hellish a mortgage application can be, we created a nightmare scenario with hundreds of thieving hands taking our character's wallet, his loose change, and finally his soul. "Traditionally animated frame by frame, the spot plays the crazy aesthetics against the grown-up subject matter of mortgage applications."

records.title: VAUXHALL ASTRA ULTIMATE "CINDERELLA"
records.description: Director Gabriel Nobrega and the Lobo crew conjure a mix of stop-motion, miniature sets, and CG to flip a fairytale into a riches-to-rags romp while high-lighting benefits of the backup camera on the Vauxhall Astra.

records.title: BOXING CAT "FIRST BLOOD"
records.description: Buenos Aires animation studio Le Cube, prodco Final Frontier, and agency R/GA Shanghai reteam on a rampaging brand film for China's Boxing Cat Brewery starring Louis, a pugilistic super-hero of suds. R/GA Shanghai ECD Terence Leong: "We were in love with Wes Anderson's Fantastic Mr. Fox and we originally wanted Louie to be a charismatic and suave stop-motion puppet with a persona like Muhammad Ali. But we couldn't find the right voice for his trash talk. Then Shing played the Spiderman theme song and boom! Everything clicked - he's a superhero who fights boring beers." Le Cube director Ralph Karam: "In developing Louie's design, adapting him from the initial 3D plan into a 2D aesthetic, we decided to use a halftone effect to create a retro comic book feel. "It was a fine line to have him embody all the wit, coolness, and self-assured confidence of Muhammad Ali, and retain the essential humor, but without creating any sense of menace that could too easily have come across."

records.title: MOUNTAIN DEW "GREEN MEANS GO"
records.description: Robert Sethi, director at The Mill in Los Angeles: "The project started with an exciting idea from BBDO Guerrero, the client's agency: The hero of the commercial, a motocross biker, puts on a pair of AR goggles and reality then augments into an epic adventure as he rides into the waves. "Myself, Brent Bonacorso (creative consultant), and the team further explored the concept to develop components of the augmented world and create a visceral adventure inspired by a video game. "The key creative challenge was weaving the narrative together in such a short duration, condensing the action down to 30 seconds while still making sure the augmented reality twist clearly came out. "It was also important the sense of gamification came across. We needed to properly establish our hero drinking, riding, racing, reaching for the prize of a Mountain Dew bottle, and then coming back to reality to celebrate with his friends. "We wanted to inject the entire spot with adrenaline and that feel of increasing momentum, pushing towards the exciting end. "We worked with incredible riders and stuntmen to shoot all the stunts in Buenos Aires. Shooting authentic stunts ensured the piece was grounded in reality. "It was key to get the raw intensity, grit, and minute detail of the motocross rider traveling through the track, navigating the environment and making the movements seem as natural as possible. "Then, in compositing, the actor needed to be rotoscoped out of all the shots and integrated back into the massive CG water landscape – his augmented reality. "This was a detailed and intensive undertaking to replace the jumps with water simulation. Of course, we also can't forget about the "little fish" – a.k.a. the massive shark! "This was an exciting challenge that took a lot of research to get just right. There was plenty of tweaking in the animation to make the shark the right size, to nail down its movements, and to have it traveling at an appropriate speed. "The shark's visibility in the water was also a conversation, as we needed the actions to be balanced to create that suspense we were looking for. "The shark pushes the narrative to the next level, adding an extra element of danger. Its presence elevates the intensity and suspense, and it becomes the end of level boss in the augmented universe. "In terms of shooting, there was an Alexa camera, Solaris with stabilized camera rig, Phantom camera, camera mounted on a dirt bike, and then equipment required for the stunts such as ramps, water pools, green screen, and wire rigs. "In terms of software, we utilized Nuke, Flame, Maya, and Houdini."

records.title: KETEL ONE "THE JOURNEY"
records.description: Creative directors Guido Lambertini, Rodier Kidmann, and Carmen Angelillo at Niceshit Studio in Barcelona, Spain: "[The agency] FIG had designed a print campaign and we entered as the animation studio to this project with one purpose: give life to this exquisite world filled with wit, a charm, and humor. "We had to develop a huge set of characters and backgrounds to narrate these magical stories into animated films, for a combination of TVC's, Social and PR films "Simplicity was a key all over this project, everything should have a feeling of approachable ease and looseness. Many times we found ourselves taking out elements instead of adding details. "With such an imperfect and hand-made style, our main focus was on the acting and timing in the scenes as we wanted to communicate as much expression possible with very few and detailed movements. "The goal was to create a bespoke and functional animated universe that hopefully will become an iconic and long-running look for the brand. "This PR film called 'The Journey' was the most difficult as we had to complete a 45-second film in two weeks from scratch. And we wanted it to be more complex than the rest of the films, i.e. camera movements and rotating buildings. "It is not every day that we receive scripts like this one, where the fine and clever humor is the key, looking for the small pauses, timing, and subtle expressions. "Also working with such a loose style, as if the stories were created on hundreds of bar napkins. It was great and fun a challege for our creativity and gathered a lot of talented people to make it come true." Schedule: Two months.

records.title: HP "MAGIC CARPET"
records.description: Co-director Alan Smith at Nexus Studios in London: "While we're all dutifully locked away in our homes, we wanted to take people on a fun-filled adventure, an escape from the current everyday restrictions re-focused on the tools that can spark imagination. "We hope this father-daughter journey of discovery resonates with the many families seeking inventive ways to inspire their little ones. "Quite the adventure for us too, being our first completely virtual and remote collaboration, which, as long as the WiFi held up, ran surprisingly smoothly."

records.title: BUDVAR "B33"
records.description: Vaclav Sladek, executive producer at Creative Embassy in Prague, Czech Republic: "The client and agency wanted to create a commercial out of gifs with different film techniques but otherwise the brief was very open. "The idea was to stir up the usually conservative beer market with something weird. Therefore this project was a mixture of different filmmaking approaches and techniques based on the beer world. "We had to execute more vignettes than is seen in the spot, because none of us had a clue how it will work in the final edit. So the main goal was to create a bank of vignettes and play with them all then fit in the music. "The first two months we were developing the list of vignettes with the agency. The execution itself was quite fast, around a month. Then we spent 2-3 weeks in the edit to finish the final piece.

records.title: LEGO "DRIVE WHAT YOU LOVE"
records.description: The imagination of a young Lego builder kicks into overdrive in this VFX-intensive spot created for The LEGO Agency by HighlyUnlikely director David Mellor and the Framestore crew. The VFX work included CG environments, cars, and digi-doubles of drivers as well as the flour explosion based on footage of rally vehicles tearing across the red mudflats of Peru's Arequipa region. Framestore took data scans and photogrammetry passes of the house location to replicate the environments in a macro scale for the CG. As well as compositing live-action shots of the McLaren and Ferrari F8 into the live-action or CG environments, the Framestore team also rebuilt the cars in CG and their LEGO counterparts. These assets were used in shots that required the cars to tear around underneath dining room chairs or across countertops. Framestore VFX supervisor Charlie Bayliss: "The cars and their drivers shift multiple times between live-action and CG digi-doubles and it's a real testament to our team's work that it's almost impossible to spot the difference between them." Lego versions of all of the other cars were also created for easter egg moments throughout the ad and for the final sequence under the kitchen stools due to the impossibility of filming a location at such scale. Director David Mellor: "Planning was key to this technical project. From experience, I knew that ensuring we consider all the aspects through to finish would, in turn, build the smoothest and best result for the film."

records.title: PORSCHE "POP STAR"
records.description: Director Chace Hartman at Scholar in New York: "The ask was to introduce the brand new 2020 Porsche 911 in a fun and exciting way by crafting a spot featuring a wide variety of 911 themed memorabilia. "The client wanted to show that the 911 isn't just a car, it's a part of pop culture. You don't need to own one to be a massive fan of the car, so the spot needed to appeal to fans of all types, not just existing owners. "With that, we needed to create a design solution that could embrace any and all representations of the iconic 911 – a variety of body styles, merchandise, fan made artwork, you name it. "We were so excited by this design challenge and opportunity to show this decades-spanning cultural icon that we wanted to do nothing more than make it f-ing awesome! "The most interesting and creative challenging aspect of the project was to create a design solution that could embrace every version of the 911. "The scope of its cultural influence has touched literally everything so getting familiar with all of that history and then choosing specific items to focus on was a challenge. "Whether it be a small paper clip silhouette, a pen holder, or a rubber ducky toy, our design solution needed to effortlessly embrace any and every possibility. What we created needed to appeal to a larger audience as well as the Porsche enthusiast that would know what was (and wasn't) authentic. "One of the main technical challenges was creating a design solution that would allow us to represent the 911 from something that was very small, to something relatively big, in any medium and form. "From live action, to poster art, to Christmas ornaments, to video games, we needed to create a system with the ability to showcase the iconic silhouette of the 911 over its evolution in an instant. "To do this, we took a less is more thought process. The iconic characteristic of the 911 is its sleek and elegant design. An absolutely unmistakable silhouette that is a constant over its multiple decade legacy. "We created a design template which locked that iconic silhouette in scale and proportion within multiple design deliverable aspect ratios to accommodate any and all of the 911's various design evolutions. "We created a universal template that solved this. When we shot live action at any scale, we set the template that projected the 911 silhouette's position and scale, and then matched it. "We used the same guidelines designing in 2D, 3D, and mixed media. When we brought the designs together into a conform, the iconic silhouette was in perfect registration no matter what culturally influential manifestation it was created in over the years.
