"The film also needed to align with the client's vision for the product launch at the Salone del Mobile trade show in Milan. "The biggest creative challenge was balancing the various elements: the furniture components, the oversized megastructure, the vibrant color palette, and the sunny, blue-sky aesthetic. "The megastructure inherently introduced a sense of chaos, and instead of fighting it, we leaned into that madness. "Our creative approach emphasized options, multiplicity, fun, and creativity — very much in line with the client's emphasis on "playful." "Another creative priority was introducing fabric as a new material in the USM Haller system. "We started with free-flowing textile to communicate tactility, then contrasted it with solid metal, ending with the ball joints shaping the final magnetic panels. "The technical challenge was to ensure accuracy at every scale and camera angle while handling the complexity of the megastructure. "We avoided using multiple levels of detail to keep the workflow consistent, which gave us complete freedom during R&D without risking inaccuracies. "To solve this, we built a USM Haller system builder HDA where each module existed as its own node. This allowed us to manipulate and animate individual modules while preserving the procedural integrity of the larger system. "For efficiency, Redshift proxies were used for most geometry, with rods generated procedurally through sweeps and curves. This setup ensured real-time viewport playback and fast rendering." Schedule: Seven weeks.

records.title: VAN RYSEL "INFERNO"
records.description: Virgile Machala and Maria Markova, producers at Eddy in Paris: "Van Rysel needed a bold, unconventional film to launch their new RCR-F INFERNO capsule, a line of high-performance cycling gear. "The goal was double: present their most advanced bike in action, and deliver a sensory, visceral experience that would resonate with cyclists. "Instead of following traditional premium codes, they asked for something more instinctive, more physical, something that could embody speed, pressure, and obsession. "The brief left a lot of room for interpretation, which allowed us to build a metaphorical, immersive vision of Hell, seen from inside a rider's mind. "The main challenge was to find the right balance between narrative ambition and raw emotional impact. "We wanted to convey both the technical precision of elite cycling and the trance-like state of exhaustion athletes experience in competition. "Animation gave us the freedom to push the sensory sliders: speed lines, distortion, visual repetition, metaphorical creatures like Cerberus or serpents, we crafted a hallucinated final lap. "We built the entire film around a single, continuous shot, a dynamic, flowing camera that never stops moving around the rider. "This meant coordinating angles, transitions, and scaling in a seamless way, all while preserving rhythm and clarity. "The animation itself was intentionally raw: expressive drawings, a restricted palette (black, red, orange, grey, white), and grainy textures helped us go fast and stay coherent with the tone. "Every element—visual or sound—had to serve the physicality and tension of the ride. "The project was completed in less than two months. From writing and storyboarding to animation, compositing, and sound, everything moved at a high pace. "The urgency matched the film's subject: a hypnotic sprint, built in the same energy. We embraced a flexible, collaborative rhythm—progressing on all fronts simultaneously, with constant dialogue between the director, artists, and the Van Rysel team. "For animation, we primarily used Adobe Animate and After Effects. This setup allowed for a fast and flexible workflow, well-suited to the expressive, textured aesthetic we were aiming for. "Sound design was crafted by Sodasound, who worked closely with us to create an immersive, narrative audio track centered on breathing, wind, and mechanical tension. "We used minimal music—most of the storytelling comes from the soundscape and a voice-over that feels like a devilish coach inside the rider's head." Schedule: Two months.

records.title: GALAXY "THE KENZ VAULT"
records.description: Javier Vallejo García, founder/CD at JVG in Madrid: "The client asked us to create a visually stunning commercial that conveyed the luxurious and indulgent essence of their Galaxy chocolate. "The brief emphasized sculptural elegance and a sense of artistic craftsmanship, highlighting the luxury aspect. "As this was a director's cut, the main challenge was finding a balance between creating something that truly resonated with us while remaining faithful to the original piece. "Striking that balance is never easy. In this case, we chose to move away from the heavy use of gold present in the original version and opted instead for a cleaner visual language. "This was paired with an original audio track, which, as usual, we produced entirely in-house. "On the technical side, the challenge was again about balance: we wanted to explore new creative solutions without overcomplicating the production in ways that would significantly delay publication. "We used simulations at several points, but in a measured way, enough to add impact and sophistication while ensuring the project remained streamlined and didn't take focus away from the next commercial production on our slate. "We approached the chocolate as if it were a sculpture in a museum. The goal was to elevate a familiar product into an artistic and almost surreal experience, turning everyday indulgence into something iconic. "In the end, we achieved a result that emphasized both innovation and luxury, which perfectly aligned with the brand's vision." Schedule: Eight weeks.

records.title: TELSTRA "INTRODUCING ROAMâ¦"
records.description: Darren Price, ECD at Mighty Nice in Sydney: "This film is all about the creative process. In this instance 'the idea' is born in the shower and then grows, gets inspired, meets some challenges and then ultimately keeps on pushing forward. "The creative brief from the agency was to create a multimedia art direction which changed style, rendering and texturing in every scene - as the idea evolves and develops." "The client had a big vision that we loved, but it took the full bag of tricks to bring it to life." "The nature of the spot - an ever-changing journey with a central character, seemed like a great opportunity to experiment with new tools and techniques. "The first solution the team came up with was to use image cards and projection mapping to create depth without full 3D builds. Mike Lomas, head of studio: "Using our initial sketches, AI was then used in some of the more photo-real scenes to generate background images. These were then projection-mapped as a major workflow accelerator. " It was interesting to see which styles AI worked well for and then which it wasn't suitable for at all, such as the cloud scene. A shallow depth of field was deliberately chosen to blur the backgrounds and reduce the need for high-detail assets. "The character was animated traditionally, but we kept the movement to a horizontal path up until the final scene which really helped with scene building. "One of the biggest challenges turned out to be one of the most foundational animation challenges: the character walk cycle. "Our hero character is the letter R, and finding the right way for it to walk took the most R&D as our animators finally found a walk cycle that gave Roamy a full range of motion while preserving the logo's side-on R shape." Darren Price: "The biggest highlight of the project is that it was one of those rare ones that brought everyone in the studio together, 2D, 3D, design and Jason, our in-house IT specialist, got to flex their chops. "It also fosters a fun and collaborative creative environment, which is what running an animation studio is really all about."

records.title: BEATS BY DRE "HUNGRY VEAR"
records.description: Colle Ignacio Godoy, EP at BUDA.tv in Buenos Aires: "The idea was to bring Vear, a character created by Japanese artist Verdy, to life for the Beats headphones. "The result was a series of pieces in which Beats and Verdy join forces in a collaboration that seamlessly blends music, urban culture, and avant-garde design. A perfect expression of the Beats spirit. "One of the biggest challenges we faced was translating Vear, a 2D character full of Verdy's signature gestures, attitude and street energy, into a 3D being that could exist convincingly in a rich, tangible world. "It wasn't just about modeling or texturing. It was about preserving his essence, the looseness of the line, the emotion in each pose and making sure that once he stepped into three dimensions, he still felt alive, touchable and undeniably Verdy. "Every detail, from his proportions to the way light interacts with his materials, was crafted to keep that balance between animation and reality, design and soul. "The production timeline spanned 12 weeks, covering the development of both the teaser and the first spot. "The response from Verdy's team was overwhelmingly positive. They embraced the character, the story and the visual style from the very beginning. "That enthusiasm fueled the entire process, keeping the energy high and pushing everyone involved to keep raising the bar until we reached the finish line. "The overall production was handled in Blender, which served as the backbone for layout, modeling, and rendering. Maya was used for animation. Meanwhile, all graphic design and compositing were developed within Adobe Creative Suite."

records.title: ON "CLOUDBOOM MAX"
records.description: Bristol-based illustrator/animator Con McHugh combines forces with digital design studio TwoMuch to add a little attitude to ON's premium marathon running shoe, the Cloudboom Max. Con McHugh: "Internally, ON had been playing with the shoe itself being this likeable, friendly character with sketched-on arms. "The campaign would be led by a 60-second video where Max would introduce himself and demonstrate all his cool tech. "The creative team at ON had a voice over scripted and some reference images. They had a huge amount of trust in letting me explore how we'd animate this character — not just what he was doing, but what he looked like and how he moved. "Drawing hands is, for many illustrators, their Achilles' heel, they avoid drawing hands and feet at all costs. "Of course, when ON approached me, this went round and round in my head, ‘This is hands, Conor — you'll be specifically drawing 60 seconds' worth of hands'. "We looked at floating hands (Rayman style), gloved hands (a la Mickey Mouse), we looked at the nature of how they moved. "The final style was a loving mix: thick and bouncy, a bit squishy, and drawn with just enough naivety to feel like street art, or something torn from my sketchbook. "The next stages of the project played out like this: storyboard, then a super rough animatic, which I passed to TwoMuch to whip up into an incredible 3D render. "It was a bit like tennis from then on — they'd send it back to me, I'd do some tests, suggest pacing tweaks, then back again — until we had something perfectly timed to the voice over and ready for the frame-by-frame animation. "I spent days locked into a routine, working from morning ‘til midnight. Maybe a sandwich, or a quick stroll round Bristol Harbor — just enough to stop me hallucinating arms on everything I looked at. "When it finally got to the stage where we combined the 3D, 2D, and TwoMuch's sound design — it was magic."

records.title: "MACARONESIAN GIN"
records.description: Gustavo Ponce, director at TAVO Studio in Madrid: "Originally, the client just wanted an animated key visual of the bottle in a cave moving subtly. "But we responded with a storytelling video, adding more details and elements to transport viewers to the brand's roots in the Canary Islands. "The film transforms the Islands' minerals, lava, water, and wildlife into the stars of a surreal narrative that beautifully links nature with design. "The creative journey involved experimenting with 3D textures, simulations, and cutting-edge lighting techniques to achieve a premium and unique outcome. "Perhaps the most challenging aspect was achieving the animals' meticulous animation and texturing. Also, achieving a look and feel that straddles realism and illustration." Schedule: Two months.

records.title: BOLL & BRANCH "LET EXTRAORDINARY TAKE OVER"
records.description: CD Miguel Rato​ and the CG specialists at Steelworks team with live action production duo Rebecca and Kevin Joelson for this dreamy take on comfort and sleep for luxury bedding brand Boll & Branch. ECD Chago Venable at Steelworks: "We collaborated closely with The Joelsons' live-action team to help shape a warm, inviting visual world, enhancing beautifully shot footage with animated CGI floral elements that evoke softness, growth, and seasonal renewal. "The client version was tailored to meet the campaign's commercial needs, while our director's cut expands on the original with extended floral animation, refined pacing, and a more immersive tone that showcases the expressive potential of CGI. "During the pre-shoot R&D phase, we used fully CGI-built rooms to explore lighting, composition, and styling. This helped to visualize the tone and pacing of the final film before the cameras rolled. "These virtual sets allowed us to test ideas, align creative direction, and ensure a seamless transition between the live-action shoot and the final integrated visuals. "By taking ownership of how live-action and CG would work together, we ensured the footage was captured with precision, resulting in a cohesive, elevated final film where practical and digital elements feel naturally unified." "To bring the concept of natural renewal to life, our team conducted extensive R&D focused on the behavior and choreography of blooming flowers. "We studied time-lapse photography, growth patterns, and petal mechanics to develop animations that felt both organic and elevated. "Building on our blooming animation system, we developed a layered choreography of movement throughout the film. "Each flower's growth served as the foundation for additional motion, petals unfurling into light, stems weaving gently through the space, and floral clusters cascading in carefully timed waves. "In the early stages of the project, we used AI tools to rapidly explore visual directions and floral compositions. "These generative references helped us iterate quickly on mood, form, and spatial arrangement, which provided a creative springboard before entering full 3D production. "Our team led the creative and visual direction for the live-talent shoot, shaping key decisions around framing, lighting, and set design to ensure every moment aligned with our planned CGI integration. "By taking ownership of how live-action and CG would work together, we ensured the footage was captured with precision, resulting in a cohesive, elevated final film where practical and digital elements feel naturally unified."

records.title: VIVOBAREFOOT "FREE YOUR FEET" MANIFESTO
records.description: Daniele Gavatorta, director at Nerdo Studio in Turin, Italy: "This project was born from a simple but powerful idea: we're all born barefoot. And being barefoot means being free – respecting the natural shape that Mother Nature gave our feet. VivoBarefoot is a bold brand that decided to team up with an equally bold agency, Thingy&Thingy, UK. They reached out with a clear statement: ‘we don't want a f**ing commercial'. "What they wanted was a manifesto, a call for change, a tool to wake people up and help them live differently. A philosophy against BigShoes: FREE Your FEET. "Our goal was to create a unique visual language, one that stayed far away from the shiny CGI worlds we usually see in big shoe brand advertising. "Instead, we wanted something imperfect, human, natural, analog. To do that, I reached out to friends and artists (mainly illustrators and animators) each with a strong handmade approach. "Techniques ranged from cut-out and collage to traditional animation and experiments with scanners to create distortions and glitches. "The result is 30 unique scenes, each completely different in style. The big challenge was making all these voices live together in one coherent flow that could still tell a story. "So a majority of pre-production focused on storyboard and animatic work, finding the best transitions and keeping the action and subject at the center. "This approach gets even trickier when you're telling a non-linear story, where each scene is more about emotions, moods, or symbolic moments rather than a straight narrative. Having a clear, big-picture vision is the first step. "Another fun challenge was that the client loved the animation but also wanted to see some live action shots. We didn't have the time or resources for a full shoot, so AI became super helpful in generating a few shots."

records.title: PUMA "SPEEDCAT"
records.description: The last time director Anton Shavkero and his CLAN crew teamed with CG studio AVE they unleashed esports madness for BetBoom (Stash 173). Now they've applied their unhinged 3D thinking to this future-pop racer vision for PUMA's classic Speedcat sneaker. The spot was produced thru agency OZIO for Russian online sports retailer Amazing Red with a soundtrack by Moscow-based composer Deem Muratov.

records.title: HUBLOT "BIG BANG 20 YEARS"
records.description: Therese Detje, co-founder/CD at Zünc Studio in London: "Hublot celebrated a milestone year in 2025, the 20th anniversary of their iconic Big Bang watch. "They were planning a big showcase at the annual Watches & Wonders convention held in Geneva, and asked us to create a hero film and other deliverables for their larger global campaign as well. "The brief itself was open, with no storyboard or styleframes to start from, which is the kind of creative challenge we love. "It means we can explore various routes, try new techniques, test out different edits and moods, and surprise the client with a rich selection of R&D to discuss and develop further. "So we had a lot of freedom, as long as we covered a few important starting points: outer space (including a literal Big Bang), conceptualizing material innovation in a lab world, and introducing five new timepieces for the limited anniversary editions. "The trickiest part was distilling a lot of ideas, worlds, and watches into one cohesive film. We were careful not to make a film that was simply a montage of cool-looking shots. "It took many, many different edits for us to find the right flow of the film, to make sure we had a continuous story that made sense. "Especially since we had two worlds, the cosmos and the laboratory, it was really fun to figure out how on earth (ha!) we could design seamless transitions between them. "I think it really helps that we're a small and nimble team who all work in-house in our London studio. "We were constantly going over to each other's desks to discuss new edits and transitions, describing the motion with our own sound effects and gestures. "It helped us come up with new shot ideas, and ditch the ones that weren't working. That's how you get those money shots - the moments that make people stop and go ‘whoa, what was that?' "The watches didn't exist physically when we started. We got our first reference photos of the actual product three days before our delivery. So, we worked from the CAD files, material guides, and a lot of back and forth with Hublot's product manager. "To get the models looking absolutely hyper-real, there was a lot of nuance in the shaders we built, for example, dialing in exactly how deep and in what direction the brushed grain should go on metal parts. "It was our first watch project, and let me tell you that these products are way more complicated than any car models that we've worked on in the past. "One technical challenge was keeping the watch asset optimized. With 730+ parts, each with its own texture and microbevel, we had to be smart with keeping file sizes down to minimize loading times and keep render times as efficient as possible. "We worked mainly in Cinema 4D with Octane render, with a little bit of help from Houdini for some simulations. We edited in After Effects, where we also did comping and color grading." Schedule: Eight weeks.

records.title: AG1 "FLAVORS"
records.description: Chapman Bullock, CD/founder at Proper in Austin, Texas: "Our first brief from the client read ‘For the first time ever, AG1 will be available in flavored alternatives including Tropical, Berry, and Citrus. How do we represent these flavors visually?' "One of the creative challenges was ensuring viewers didn't assume each AG1 flavor was a different colored drink. AG1 is always the same signature green. "To emphasize this, we made the clear bottle filled with the green beverage the visual hero as it moved through various scenes—reinforcing that the color remains consistent across all flavors. "Since the bottle is in constant motion, this introduced a technical challenge with how the CG fluid behaved. Edu and Diego did an excellent job planning for this, making sure the contents inside the bottle reacted in a natural and realistic way. "We ended up using four different fluid simulations. In certain cases, we took the approach of simulating the liquid in a static bottle and adjusting the direction of gravity to control the motion. "This technique allowed us to repurpose a single sim across multiple shots, streamlining the process without sacrificing realism." "In addition to social and YouTube platforms, the film is also airing on broadcast TV. The client also extracted 4K stills from the project for use in billboards and print. " Schedule: Two months. Two to three weeks for design and R&D, six weeks for animation.

records.title: BENTLEY "MADE TO MOVE YOU"
records.description: Georgi Chalakov (Senior Designer) and Rebecca Scheinberg (Production Lead) at Found in London: "We were tasked with creating a series of films to highlight Bentley's three core brand pillars — Design, Craftsmanship, and Performance — showcasing both the beauty of the cars and the power beneath their refined exteriors. "The main creative challenge was using CG to capture the beauty, craftsmanship, and exceptional finish of a Bentley, especially its intricate details. "To ensure we really highlighted the time and effort that goes into manufacturing, we visited their factory to understand the process better. "We then worked to translate this into a beautiful, larger-than-life CGI world, getting up close to hero details that we would never be able to do in live action. "Our biggest technical hurdle was capturing the factory's exceptional craftsmanship, especially the embroidery process. "We spent considerable time depicting the direction of each stitch and the smoothness of every thread, ensuring their precision was clear on screen. "Another challenge was visually transforming the abstract veneer layers into the thread that begins the stitching. We aimed to show the transition from polished, glossy surfaces to soft threads in a single continuous shot, highlighting the story behind every detail. "We were inspired by the car's intricate details and wanted to bridge the real and abstract worlds in our visuals." Schedule: Eight weeks.

records.campaign_title: FRANCE TÃLÃVISIONS "MILAN CORTINA 2026 OLYMPIC & PARALYMPIC GAMES"
records.description: Paris VFX force Mathematic and LA/PAC director Quentin Deronzier, who also brought us the Dacia spot in this issue, delivers a dream-like action promo for the 2026 Winter Olympics on French public broadcaster France Télévisions. Quentin Deronzier: "The Italian Alps are right next door to where I grew up. Having been surrounded by winter sports since childhood, I've always seen the mountains as an endless playground, and that's exactly what I wanted to capture in this film. "The film's snow sculptures pay tribute to timeless names of Italian art, including Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci, and Botticelli, as well as the mountains of the games' host cities Milan and Cortina d'Ampezzo."

records.title: DACIA "HIPSTER"
records.description: The VFX and 3D animation crews at Mathematic in Paris team with LA/PAC director Quentin Deronzier to stage this full-CG show-stopper for Dacia's diminutive new Hipster Concept EV through agency Publicis Conseil. Quentin Deronzier: "The idea was to push the contrast between a small car and the colossal machines surrounding it to the maximum. "Starting from a concept as simple as it is effective, I had the freedom to build something grand and visually powerful." From Mathematic: "The Dacia film required us to merge technical precision with creative intent, designing an immense CG factory where every element moved in harmony. "The challenge lay in crafting a magisterial mechanical world while keeping the compact car at the center of attention. "Each robotic gesture and lighting cue was timed to perfection, creating a seamless rhythm. "In close collaboration with Quentin Deronzier and Publicis Conseil, we turned engineering into choreography, delivering a film that unites industrial power with cinematic grace."

records.title: FIERCE MILD BREWING CO. "BREW THINGS DIFFERENTLY"
records.campaign_title: FIERCE MILD BREWING CO. "BREW THINGS DIFFERENTLY"
records.description: Director Alex Dron and Yukfoo Animation in Auckland deliver wonderfully eccentric character work here for the first TV campaign from Irish non-alcoholic beer brand Fierce Mild. Alex Dron: "This spot is the result of Fierce Mild winning the inaugural Love Irish Food × Sky Media Taste of TV Fund. "As part of this win, they were awarded a fully-funded TV campaign and media investment to bring the brand's story to screens nationwide. "The plan was to highlight the character of the non-alcoholic beer by showing their mascot letting his personality out in everyday situations." "It turns out creativity ferments in ironic conditions. Yukfoo EP, Alan Dickson, and Public House CD, Colin Hart, first discussed the animation over a glass of wine at Annecy. "Despite the product being non-alcoholic, it was a requirement that the animation not appeal to children. "The solutions for this were multi-faceted, for example, using smaller eyes and mouths, keeping out of fun kid environments, and not doing activities that might traditionally be for young people. The relaxed brand colors were also perfect for the brief. "Another consideration was the budget. We needed a simple approach that was effective to execute economically. "2D rigged animation worked well for this, and it was paired with simple background designs."

records.title: INFINITUM "CHRISTMAS COMMERCIAL 2025"
records.description: Martin Engh, director and co-owner of ADP in Oslo, Norway: "The brief from the agency was to tell an emotional story about a family of mice who find shelter in an empty plastic bottle. "It's a warm and cozy story until the bottle falls over and we realise that the mice won't be able to get out. This is a real problem in nature. "Initially, the challenge was convincing the client that traditional 2D cel animation still has a place in mass communication. Thankfully, the agency team at Pulse championed the vision all the way, giving us the freedom to do things the right way. "One of the biggest creative challenges was shaping the ending of the film. The story required a sudden and dramatic tonal shift, as the bottle that serves as the mice's home tips over, trapping them inside and ultimately leading to their death. "The challenge was to make this moment emotionally impactful without moving into melodrama, and to clearly communicate the outcome without explicitly showing it. "One of the technical challenges was maintaining stylistic consistency while working with a large team of background artists and animators. "Another technical challenge was defining the look of the bottle's interior, translating its roundness and distortion. "Another deliberate choice, rather than a challenge per se, was to limit the use of shadows and highlights to achieve the look of an older animated film. "Contemporary animation often relies heavily on lighting, shading, and effects, but for this project, the characters were kept relatively flat to get a classic cartoon feel. In contrast, the backgrounds were rendered with a high level of detail."

records.title: XIAOMI "LOVE STORY"
records.description: Álvaro Ibáñez, project manager at Kutuko Studio in Madrid: "Xiaomi came to us with a beautiful idea: dust bunnies. "They were clear from the start that they wanted to communicate the product from an emotional and accessible angle, not through the typical tech-heavy messaging. "From there, our job was to take that spark and turn it into a full story. "We shaped the narrative, built the arc, the tone, and that little love story that turns two balls of dust into soulful protagonists… without giving them eyes or turning them into cartoon characters. "The biggest challenge was telling a lot in a very short amount of time. We wanted the audience to connect with the dust bunnies within seconds. "We also had to find a delicate balance: making the bunnies realistic, with texture and weight, but still adorable and emotional, without falling into classic character anthropomorphization. "Achieving that emotional realism was a huge challenge. Dust bunnies are chaotic masses, full of microfibers, dynamics, and complex physical behavior. "They needed to look natural, yet still readable as characters. We went through extensive R&D, grooming tests, and simulation exploration to find that exact point where they remain dust, but they express something. "From concept, narrative, animatics, lookdev, simulations, animation, to post-production, the process took four months. A very careful, handcrafted workflow with lots of iteration to match the emotional sensitivity the brand was looking for. "We worked in Cinema 4D with the Redshift render engine, which gave us great control over lighting and the fine detail of the dust bunnies. Post-production was done in DaVinci Resolve, and sound design in Ableton. "At a time when AI can generate images and videos at absurd speeds, what truly makes a difference are stories with intention, with meaning, pieces crafted with care. "That mindset, betting on narrative, on the human element, is what allows two dust bunnies to tell a story that resonates globally."

records.title: XFINITY "RABBITS"
records.description: Blinkink directors Andy Biddle and Adeena Grubb (aka Andy & Adena) pack this stop-motion opus for internet service provider Xfinity with warmth, whimsy, and the benefits of fast WiFi for a very large and furry family. Andy Biddle: "As soon as we read the script and brief, we knew it was something special. "We wanted to really lean into that tactile, handcrafted quality, the kind that gives films like Fantastic Mr Fox (which I had the pleasure of animating on) its unique charm everyone loves. "From a technical standpoint, the approach was actually refreshingly pure. Everything was done in-camera with minimal post-production. "If you see seven rabbits in a shot, that's because we truly did animate all seven, together in the shot." Adeena Grubb: "It was incredible seeing the rabbit home pieced together for the final shot, it was almost 12 feet tall! "The amount of detail that went into this one is mind-blowing; it's the kind of thing you need to watch several times over to spot all of the fun little details we embedded in the whole film."

records.title: GUERLAIN "A TALE OF WONDER"
records.description: Lucas Navarro, director and co-founder at Illogic Studios in Montpellier, France: "The story of this film was to depict an animated cut-paper world set within a perfumer's workshop. "The brief was to create a film that felt both magical and photorealistic, with a sophisticated and elegant mise-en-scène. "As with every Guerlain Christmas campaign, the artistic ambition is very high, as the elegance of the brand must come through in these films. "We were immediately drawn to the concept because we knew it had the potential to become a charming and spectacular film. "Right from the start, we were aligned with the agency on how we wanted to film this miniature world: immersive camera movements, a feeling of being swept rapidly through different universes with new surprises in every scene, and above all, freshness and poetry. "We also wanted a crescendo structure: beginning very softly and growing in scale and intensity as the film unfolds. "To make Guerlain's A Tale of Wonder as spectacular as possible, we had to overcome numerous technical challenges (the number of sets, the number of characters, FX work, etc.). "The main challenge was representing paper in 3D. To achieve a truly convincing texture, we collaborated with Marvin Büte, a German CG artist passionate about origami. "He knows how to authentically reproduce the look of crumpled, slightly folded paper, imperfect, yet incredibly charming. "This was exactly what we wanted, and he amazed us with paper hummingbirds, elephants, and chameleons that looked more real than reality itself. "To elevate the entire piece, great care was given to lighting in order to create an atmosphere that is both magical and premium. "What worked particularly well was the idea of light seeming to emanate from within the animals and spreading through the paper. "The production took nearly eight months from start to finish. Early on, we agreed with the agency to work at a slower pace, allowing us to maintain a high level of quality throughout the process. "It is also important to note that, in addition to the main film, several shorter capsule films had to be delivered."

records.title: NESPRESSO "ATELIER OF WONDER"
records.description: Shane Griffin, director at GRIF. in New York: "Our task was to design an ‘Atelier of Wonder' for Nespresso that felt like a mix between a magical factory line, a rube goldberg machine, and a high-end luxury store. "The purpose of the atelier was to show how all of the flavors, accessories, and a wide array of products get created, packed, and shipped in time for the festive season. "The creative challenge was to design a series of little technical machines that actually worked together to transport our products through the atelier in a whimsical & surprising way. "These machines had to be functional, yet charming, while also adding a sense of premium quality, exuding a warm, festive feeling. "It felt more akin to engineering than a motion design project, as every little decision had a knock-on effect further down the conveyor belt. "There was a heavy modeling and look development period, specifically getting the foams of the various different types of coffees correct – each recipe has a different ratio of coffee to milk, and different preparation, so the crema (or foam) changes color, density, and height. "We rendered with Redshift, and used mostly a blend between an SSS shader (for any milky coffee or foam) and a standard liquid shader (for transparent coffee). "But that was just the static assets; the coffee pours themselves needed a new approach entirely. "Let's take the milk pouring into the glass, and then the coffee pouring into the milk, that is an extremely difficult sim to begin with, now pair that with the action of it dynamically moving on a conveyor belt with mechanical arms that pick it up and swing it around, and let's add some ice cubes on top of that! "It was very tricky. We used a blend of Phoenix, Embergen, TyFlow, After Effects, and Redshift procedural shaders to pull off that shot. "Then came the machinery. Some of it relied on physics, some of it relied on kinematic systems, and some relied on good old-fashioned keyframes. "There really was no blueprint or reference point here; we blocked out the action using simple geometry, but when it came to building them out, we made a concerted effort to architect them in a way that could physically work in the real world. "For the most part, all the cogs, wheels, and levers were rigged up to work correctly, so if you look closely, everything makes sense." Schedule: Five months.

records.title: SPECSAVERS "THE RELATIONSHIP AID"
records.description: Ambrogio Bergamaschi, creative lead at Found in London: "The brief was deceptively simple: launch a nearly invisible hearing aid for Specsavers in a way that would genuinely capture attention. "The real challenge wasn't functional; it was cultural. Hearing aids are often marketed in a clinical way, which can unintentionally reinforce stigma. "The ambition was to reframe the device as something desirable and intimate, positioning it not as a medical necessity, but as a catalyst for connection. "Golin London approached us with a tongue-in-cheek concept: present the hearing aid as ‘the device your relationship has been missing', a couple's connection device. "The idea stemmed from a strong writing-led insight that connection sits at the heart of both relationships and hearing. "By leaning into ambiguity and borrowing the visual language of a different category, we could intrigue audiences and play with perception before revealing the truth. "The film was to be fully realised in 3D, with slow, deliberate movement, sensual lighting, and tactile materials to create an intimate arena. "Voiceover would play a central role in reinforcing the connection narrative, while the visuals were crafted to keep the audience guessing. "On paper, it was a simple brief. In execution, it required nuance, something provocative enough to spark conversation, yet art-directed with taste and restraint to feel elevated rather than sensational. "The biggest creative challenge was striking the right balance between suggestion and reveal. "The entire idea depended on ambiguity, showing just enough to spark a specific assumption, but never so much that the illusion collapsed too early. "It required constant calibration: build intrigue, keep it tasteful, and don't give the game away. "It was about holding the entire piece together: the edit, the pacing, the music, the voiceover. Every element needed to pull in the same direction. "Technically, the piece wasn't about complexity; it was about consistency. We worked across multiple lighting setups while maintaining a single, coherent visual language. "The cinematography had to feel intimate and sculpted, yet still believable. Holding that tone across different environments required precision and restraint. "On a project like this, subtlety is the technical challenge. The craft has to disappear so the audience stays immersed in the story. "One of the most surprisingly difficult decisions was choosing the music as the piece's mood shifted dramatically depending on the track. "In early edit tests, we paired the film with an '80s-style jazzy bass track. It pushed the tone so far into cheeky territory that everyone internally couldn't stop laughing. "It was a sharp reminder of how much perception is shaped by sound, and how a single musical choice can completely reframe an audience's interpretation." Schedule: Six weeks.

records.title: MACKENZIE INVESTMENTS "SEE THINGS OTHERS MISS"
records.description: Working through Toronto agency The Garden, French director/illustrator Emmanuelle Walker and WIZZ channel the style of editorial illustration into a series of surreal vignettes for one of Canada's largest investment management firms. Lindsay Eady, ECD at The Garden: "Our first campaign proved that behaving ‘out of category' captures attention. This year, we wanted to use the inventiveness of that world to bring more of Mackenzie's innovative approach to life. "Animation allowed us to make complex stories like energy transition or quantitative models clearer and more visceral while maintaining the distinctive style that builds brand recall."

records.title: ERSTE BANK "THE BIRD"
records.description: Launched in 2025 by creatives from MPC and The Mill, London VFX shop The Perlin team with directors DOM&NIC on a clever feathery escape for Austrian banking giant Erste thru Jung Von Matt Donau. DOM&NIC: "At its heart, the story is about determination, resilience, and the refusal to give up and we wanted to bring the audience along on that journey in the most entertaining, cinematic and emotionally involving way possible. "We wanted the audience to empathize with the bird as a character, but never lose the sense that this is a real bird in a real cage." From The Perlin: "One of the biggest challenges was keeping the character performance appealing without anthropomorphizing it. "The animation had to stay grounded in behavior that felt believable and true to life, so the audience could enjoy the fantasy while also feeling it could really happen. "To achieve this, the team closely studied real bird movement and built reference libraries to capture specific behaviors for each moment in the film. "The key was shaping performance, intent and timing without breaking realism. "This was supported by a bespoke feather system developed in Houdini, with hand-keyed animation driving the main body and wing performance. "A particular challenge was creating seamless transitions between open and folded wings, solved through complex simulation that allowed the feathers to fold naturally into one another."

records.title: LENOVO "THINKPAD"
records.description: Blacklist directing collective Polynoid deploy a mix of procedural animation and photo-real rendering in this thinly disguised jab at Apple while introducing the Lenovo Thinkpad laptop aimed at the no-nonsense power user. Ilija Brunck: "The Woo Agency had the idea to establish an Apple-like world and get it swallowed by our hero, the carbon fiber. What we really liked about the brief is that we could destroy something white and slick and by that making the world a darker place. "Because of the long pack shots we were left with only 15 seconds for the actual storytelling. It was quite challenging to establish the setting and tell the story of the carbon take over in this short amount of time. "The carbon fibers are created in Softimage ICE using strands. We use those strands in a lot of our productions and built a production pipeline for using it in all kind of situations. "The wonderful thing about strands is that it gives you the opportunity to procedurally create something very detailed and still design and render it quickly. Schedule: "The spot was produced in six weeks from concept to final product. In the first weeks we worked on basic animatics to nail the pacing and edit of the clip. After that we went through several rounds of redefining all the elements."

records.title: TARGET "PINK"
records.description: The first in a series of spots by Motion Theory director and co-founder Mathew Cullen for Target previewing original tracks from mainstream pop artists exclusively available at the retail giant. The campaign promotes a new initiative from Target, where best-selling artists will launch Target-specific versions of their new albums. Cullen worked with Target's in-house team to develop concepts for each spot based on the tracks themselves, together with subtle visual nods to Target's branding. "The performance sequence was captured in Los Angeles on a set adorned with reflective orbs.

records.title: PILSNER URQUELL "170 YEAR ANNIVERSARY"
records.description: French directing duo ROJO teams with Prague studio Eallin Motion Art to help mark the 170th anniversary of the creation of the Czech beer Pilsner Urquell by enhancing high-speed macro live action footage with CGI. "The challenge was to fit the idea within a budget. We did this by not creating the film fully in 3D but by shooting elements of the universe on table top then combining the 3D with the live action footage in the most believable and organic way. "The most difficult part was dynamic simulation of a rotating galaxy and fire elements. Even with the most high end technology behind you, simulating such complex phenomena is a very hard task. Especially when you require the maximum level of creative freedom and visual control which you cannot achieve during real shooting. Schedule: Six weeks.

records.title: JBL "EAR OF THE TORNADO"
records.description: Psyop Creative Director, Anh Vu: "Doner executive creative director, Murray White, had a concept for JBL's second cinematic branding spot that would fully envelop the viewer. He wanted people to witness the birth of a natural phenomenon and vividly experience the destructive sounds of mother nature. "We were aware we needed to communicate a real narrative even though we were going for a photoreal look, the spot had to be artful and carefully finessed chaos." "'Ear of the Tornado' contains around 70 million particles from start to finish. The choreography and animation of the flying and crashing objects were all designed with particular attention to the rhythm for the sound design. Psyop collaborated with Skywalker Sound to guarantee the 5.1 mix of the audio was as impactful and engrossing as possible."

records.title: DULUX "A LOT OF LIVING"
records.description: Director Pete Circuitt, Auckland, NZ: "My brief was to create an upbeat, vibrant and energetic animation technique to reflect the life that happens within the walls of our homes. "The ad was to feature a cast of characters sliding along the walls in heavily stylized, painted silhouettes, leaving behind a trail of colorful destruction that only a paint like Dulux Wash and Wear could withstand. "It was important to remain honest to the tools available for interior painting. So all the artwork is painted predominantly with a roller, with a little detail work done with a four-inch brush. We created natural digital brushes directly from what we observed when we painted on actual walls during pre-production. "Initially to limit our toolset to big rollers and broad four-inch brushes seemed like a big task but when I did the initial style frames, I found I could get a tremendous amount of detail from your average roller, and it could be made to look very cool. "We didn't paint the animation on set because it was not practical to secure any residential location for the many weeks required to do it. The action is instead painted digitally, and because it's done in computers, the real achievement lies in the trail technique. "When a character moves it leaves a history behind it. And it is this quality which was terrifically difficult to execute with tracked cameras. "Originally a story was written that observed a battle between two brother and sister 'monsters'. I was really excited to use my son's drawings as a base for the creature designs. "Although the final script changed significantly, the original monster style frames I painted informed me how to approach the project creatively. I have included a few of these for fun and because I am very fond of them. "Finally, credit must be given to the amazing animated graffiti work of BLU. His incredible work was a constant inspiration. Thank-you." Schedule: "All told we had six weeks, but only two weeks after we shot the live-action to digitally paint all the action on the walls."

records.title: DEEZER "MUSIC UNLEASHED"
records.description: Wizzdesign producer Matthieu Poirier in Paris: "The agency (Being, part of TBWA) contacted Wizz Design (the motion graphic studio of Quad) for the production of the first campaign for Deezer. The brief was to illustrate in three scenes: 'freeing music from being trapped' and the power of music by creating an animation to fit the style of (the illustrator) McBess. "The biggest challenge was to translate the very detailed illustrations supplied by McBess into motion and find a direction suited to his style. So we chose to propose the most simple and clean compositions and created the work as 2D animation so it had to be animated by hand, including every small stroke of McBess' textures. "On the other hand, we wanted to make one single shot for the entire spot so we had to find clever transitions for the animations that were linked without any cut in the staging." Schedule: one month.

records.title: NIKE "KALEIDOSCOPE"
records.description: Bryan Shrednick, director of business development for Royale in LA: "Nike came to Royale with a very simple request, to create a film that showcases the flexibility of the Nike Free 5.0 Running shoe. "Ten days later, Royale had created five independently unique concepts that showcased the flexibility of the shoe. Nike immediately selected the Kaleidoscope option, and Royale went back to the drawing board to flesh out production style frames, and later, a completely CG pre-vis. "One technical challenge was shooting the shoes live action rather than using CG. We felt this method allowed us to remain true to the original creative request from Nike. "For the live-action shoot, physically rigging the shoes to contort to the movements we desired was also a challenge. Timing the motion rig and camera movements became exponentially more difficult as the rig melted under the extremely hot studio lights. "Our main creative challenge was keeping the Kaleidoscope imagery engaging and beautiful while remaining uncluttered. When you're duplicating/reflecting the shoes, things get chaotic very quickly. Royale also produced a print campaign that has seen heavy OOH rotation. The campaign can be seen on billboards, displays at Nike stores, and displays at Nike retailers including Foot Locker and Sports Authority. Schedule: 1/31/13: Live Action Shoot 2/1/12: Editorial Prep and Rotoscoping 2/13/13: Animation 3/7/13: Final Cleanup and Color Grading 3/14/13: Final Rendering 3/21/13: Complete and Deliver Finals "Nike distributed the videos around the web, including their social media platforms, the nike.com US homepage, and various international Nike web properties. "Our favorite fan comment from YouTube has been 'I had total mindfuck after watching this commercial.' Thanks man, that's usually what we're going for. The videos can also be seen in stores as part of an interactive display and on video billboards around the world." Hardware: RED Epic, turntable rig, fishing line. Software: After Effects, Cinema 4D, REDCINE-X Pro After Effects: compositing, editing, color grading REDCINE: transcoding and color correction Cinema 4D: Match move cg shoes to the live plates to generate accurate shadows

records.title: SKULLCANDY "CRUSHER"
records.description: Wolf & Crow visualize the power of sound for the new Skullcandy Crusher headphones in this new spot starring NBA superstar Kevin Durant and Grammy-nominated rapper Wale, featuring a Wale and French Montana remix of "We Back 2 Ballin." The scope of the project, from concept to storyboard, live-action shoot to VFX, and final Flame finishing, was completed entirely by the team at Wolf & Crow at their Los Angeles studio. Skullcandy approached Wolf & Crow with the challenge of visualizing sound in a way that hadn't been seen before. Skullcandy Crushers are bass-driven headphones that physically vibrate when they are used, which the Wolf & Crow team interpreted in different manifestations throughout the spot. The ripples through Durant's skin were created by modeling Durant's head, texturing the skin on it and matching the lighting, then layering in some compositing magic to finish. Once Wale's track really kicks in, the physicality of the audio explodes out of the headphones into the environment. The VFX elements are glossy and clean, representing the aesthetic of the Crusher headphones, as well as rough and aggressive to highlight the audio power that the user experiences when wearing the headphones.

records.title: RED CROSS "PARCEL"
records.description: Holbrooks director, Daniel Gray in New York: "We wanted to take the material and create a real rollercoaster of imagery and emotion. We wanted to show how Red Cross is brave and committed in their quest to helping those in need. "The team employed a mix of cel animation and 3D camera work to balance handcrafted warmth with dynamic storytelling. "We took advantage of being located in both New York City and Budapest to maximize production days, working around the clock with the New Zealand client to manage the compressed production schedule. The spot is currently running in New Zealand as part of the Red Cross Annual Appeal."

records.title: ANCHOR MILK "COWS"
records.description: Damon Duncan, director at Assembly in Aukland, NZ: "Colenso BBDO came to Assembly with a fantastic concept for their client Anchor – the concept was based around a new package that protects the milk from being exposed to light. "The concept was to create a glass cow, desperate to keep its precious cargo away from the light. Assembly leapt at the chance to create a test to prove the concept. "This was a little less polished than the final results but gave Colenso and the team at Anchor the confidence that the idea would could work in the real world. "There were a few sleepless nights leading up to the filming as we were shooting this spot in the depths of a New Zealand winter, famous for its long, rainy days. "We were lucky enough to have good weather on the shoot days however, a blessing as the entire concept hinged on the interplay of shadows and the sun, both extremely important characters in the scripts. "We used full size cutouts of cows on the shoot so we could frame up on the correct scale within our scenes. "Ultimately we relied on cinematographer Ian McCarrol's feel for the motion we were trying to express when we were capturing our clean plates, leading the viewers to the action and endeavoring to follow the protagonists on the screen. "We made the decision very early on to keep the camera very naturalistic with a softened handheld feel, utilizing a bungee rig on the camera to achieve this. "The animation of the cows was extremely important to achieve the subtlety that we were after, injecting the right amount of character into the cows without losing their bovine qualities. "The extremely talented animation department at Assembly tackled the job with an eye to weight and gravity to ensure the large amount of volume that the cows were moving around inside them felt believable and true to the real world. "Technically this job was an enormous challenge. From the rendering of the glass to the simulation of the milk there were numerous issues to overcome. "Our pipeline started with Maya where the cow modeling, rigging and animation was done. The animation was all keyframe. Maya Muscle was used to achieve convincing skin sliding and jiggle effects while maintaining volume. "Despite the cows being made of glass, it turned out that these effects were an important part of getting the cows to appear lifelike and full of bovine character. We then used the built-in point caching to transfer the completed animation to 3ds Max. "Once inside Max, we used Thinkbox Frost to calculate the mesh from our fluid particle files that we generated in a proprietary fluid simulator. We cached the fluid meshes to the network with Thinkbox XMesh to give us fast scene interactivity. "On top of this mesh we used some custom modifiers made in Thinkbox Genome to get smooth sides and sharp edges where the milk hits the glass. "Once we had a nice milk mesh, we cached the subsurface light scattering (SSS) contribution on the milk. This means we could re-render without having to wait for the time consuming SSS calculations. It also meant that the milk surface stayed smooth and flicker free despite being refracted through the glass. "All the rendering was done using V-Ray and we used Thinkbox Deadline to manage simulation, caching, and 2D and 3D rendering tasks on our render farm. "The bird was all made in Maya with individual feather geometry. Because of the bird's rapid movement, it was animated with subframe animation so that the motion blur would reveal all the action. "All the comp work was completed in Nuke 7 using deep compositing for some of the crowd shots. Having deep renders meant we could render all the cows in one pass and then insert grass mattes in between individual cows for the grass/ground integration. "We used The Foundry Hiero to maintain a current cut of each commercial, ready for review at any time. As each shot was updated and finished, they seamlessly updated in context of the full edit. We also found it great for making tweaks to the cut right up to the deadline."

records.title: TELUS "WAKE UP"
records.description: Project lead, Chris Johnson at Topix in Toronto: "First we built a fairly exhaustive library of reference material. This allowed us to determine, on paper, which attributes would best fit our ideal TELUS spokes-critter, in collaboration with the agency and client. "We gathered numerous video clips to provide the animators with behavior and motion references. We also developed a customized production pipeline integrating the steps needed to build and rig the assets, animate them, apply textures, fur, skin and muscle dynamics, and finally render our images photo-realistically, using a carefully selected collection of both available software and our own proprietary tools. "While the design and build of the models, rigs and furring routines were time-consuming tasks, the assets are now built and available for an entire campaign and beyond. "The other great benefit is that the pipeline, documented expertise and toolsets are all in place so that we can quickly and efficiently adapt them to other new critters as they are added to the line-up." Topix animation supervisor, Marcus Alqueres: "We were constantly walking this fine line between cartoony and realistic performances, so every time we had a very specific direction, we had to stop and think about how a real animal would perform that action." Topix senior producer Cathy Jefferies: "Starting with our own core group of in-house designers, animators and project leads, we were able to assemble a dream team of very specialized talent from all over the world, most of whom have worked on large scale feature projects. At its peak, the team was up to 20 people. "Marcus is from Brazil, one of our lighters is located in Australia, one of our modelers was working remotely from Paris and New York. We also had a couple of people working out of Montreal and some animators were re-located to Toronto from Vancouver."
